than a widow in her halls, nor any feebler woman.”
So she cried aloud; but her son addressed her in answer:
“Take courage, my mother, and send away the evil omen;
for no man is slain in war beyond his fated doom;
and if it is fated for me to die for the Achaeans,
let me die, having done some deed worthy of the line of Aeacus.”
So he spoke; and near him came aged Lycomedes,
and addressed him as he longed for battle:
“O strong-hearted child, like your father in might,
I know that you are mighty and strong; yet even so
I fear the bitter war and the grievous wave
of the sea; for sailors are ever near to destruction.
But beware, child, when you come upon a voyage
hereafter, either from Troy or from elsewhere, such as often
we men wander upon the boundless back of the sea,
at the time when the sun joins the misty Goatfish,
casting behind him the Archer, drawer of arrows,
when storms drive on the grievous winter,
or when down the wide stream of Ocean are borne
the stars as Orion goes down toward the darkness;
fear in your heart the grievous equinox,
when over the wide depths of the sea
storms gather, darting from somewhere over the great gulf,
or when the setting of the Pleiades comes, which too
fear as it plunges raging into the sea, and the other
stars likewise, which are a terror to wretched men
as they set or rise over the wide stream of the sea.”
So speaking he kissed the boy, and did not bar him from the road
as he longed for the ill-sounding war; and he, with a lovely
smile, hastened to go swiftly to the ship.
But still in his mother's halls the tearful converse
held him back, eager though his feet were.
And as when a man holds back a swift horse
straining for the course, sitting upon him, and it,
champing the curbing bit, snorts, and its breast
is wet with foam, and its feet will not stand still in their longing for the road,
and about one spot, beneath its nimble feet,
as it moves quickly there is a constant clatter, and its mane
tosses as it strains, and it lifts its head on high,
snorting again and again, and the heart of its lord rejoices;
so the glorious son of war-abiding Achilles
his mother held back, but his feet hurried on;
and she, grieving though she was, gloried in her son.
And he, kissing her again and again, left her all alone,
mourning grievously through the house of her dear father;
as about the eaves a swallow, greatly grieving,
mourns her dappled young, which, chirping loud,
a dread serpent has devoured and grieved their faithful mother,
and she now flits about her widowed nest,
now flies about the well-made porch,
wailing dreadfully for her young; so for him
Deidameia mourned, and now about her son's
bed flung herself and cried aloud, now again
wept upon the door-posts; and she laid in her dear bosom,
if there was any plaything made for him in the halls,
with which, when he was little, he gladdened his tender heart;
and if anywhere she saw a javelin left behind,

title: The Fall of Troy
text:
often she kissed it, and whatever else, weeping,
she saw of her warlike son. But he, of his mother's
boundless lamentation, listened no more, but apart
went to the swift ship; and his swift limbs bore him,
like a star all shining. And about him
followed, together with wise Odysseus, the son of Tydeus,
and twenty other men, firm of heart in their spirits,
whom Deidameia held as the most trusted in her house,
and gave them to her son to be his swift squires.
They then busily attended on the bold son of Achilles
as he hastened to the ship through the city; and he in their midst
went rejoicing; and the Nereids rejoiced
about Thetis; and the Dark-Haired One himself was glad
beholding the mighty son of blameless Achilles,
how he already longed for the tearful war
though he was still a boy, still beardless; but valour
and might urged him on; and from his homeland he sped,
like Ares when he comes to the bloody battle
enraged with his foes, and his great spirit rages,
and grim is the brow above his eyes, and about him
his eyes flash like fire, and his cheeks,
clothed at once with beauty and chill terror,
ever appear as he rushes on, and the very gods tremble;
such was the goodly son of Achilles; and throughout the city
the people prayed to the immortals to bring safe their noble lord
back again from the grievous war; and they heard
their prayers. And he surpassed all who followed him.
And coming to the shore of the loud-roaring sea
they found the rowers within the well-polished ship
making ready the sails and bustling about the vessel;
and quickly they went aboard; and the others loosed the cables
and the anchor-stones, which ever attend the great strength of ships.
And to them the husband of Amphitrite granted fair sailing
willingly; for greatly in his heart he cared for the Achaeans
worn down by the Trojans and great-souled Eurypylus.
And they, sitting on either side of the son of Achilles,
delighted him with stories, telling of his father's deeds,
all that he devised on the wide voyage and on the land
of close-fighting Telephus, and all that he did to the Trojans
about the city of Priam, bringing glory to the sons of Atreus;
and his heart was warmed as he too longed
to win the glory and renown of his fearless father.
And she, somewhere in her chamber, grieving for her son,
noble Deidameia, shed many tears,
and the heart within her, beneath grievous pains,
melted as feeble lead upon the embers
or a fragment of wax; and lamentation never left her
as she gazed upon the boundless sea; because a mother
grieves for her son, even when he goes to a feast
far off, summoned by a dear man to a stranger's house.
And the sails of the ship, as it went far off,
were now hidden, and seemed like mist;
but she still groaned, lamenting all day long.
And the ship sped over the sea as the wind followed,
barely touching the much-resounding sea;
and the purple wave roared about the keel on either side;
and quickly the ship made its way across the great gulf, voyaging.
And about it fell the darkness of night; and it, beneath the wind
and the steersman, sailed on through the depths of the sea;
and divine Dawn came toward heaven.
And to them appeared the crests of the Idaean mountains,
Chrysa and the seat of Smintheus and the headland of Sigeum
and the tomb of warlike Aeacides; but in no way
did the wise-minded son of Laertes show it
to Neoptolemus, lest grief should grow
in his heart within his breast. And they passed the islands
quickly, the Calydnae; and Tenedos was left behind;

title: The Fall of Troy
text:
and again appeared the seat of Eleus, where the tomb
of Protesilaus stands, shaded by lofty elms,
which, when they behold, rising from the ground,
Ilium, at once their tops swiftly wither.
And the wind bore the rowed ship near Troy;
and it came where the other ships also lay along the shore
of the Argives, who at that time were toiling wretchedly,
fighting about the wall, which before they themselves had built
to be a bulwark of the ships and of the mighty host
in the war; but it was now, by the hands of Eurypylus,
about to be brought low, crashing to the ground,
had not the son of strong Tydeus at once perceived
the long battlements being battered; and swiftly he leapt from the swift ship,
and boldly shouted, as loud as his heart within him could hold:
“O friends, truly a great calamity rolls upon the Argives
this day; but come, quickly let us put on our gleaming arms
and go to the tumult of the laborious war;
for already against our towers are fighting
the warlike Trojans, who soon, having broken the long walls,
will most terribly burn the ships with fire;
and for us there will be no homecoming, much as our hearts long for it,
but we ourselves too, swiftly overcome beyond our doom,
shall lie in Troy, far from our children and our wives.”
So he spoke; and they swiftly leapt from the swift ship
in full force; for trembling seized all who heard,
except warlike Neoptolemus, since he was like
his dear father in great might; and desire for battle fell upon him.
And quickly they came to the hut of Odysseus;
for it was nearest to his dark-prowed ship;
and there lay many arms of exchange beside it,
both of shrewd Odysseus and of his other
godlike comrades, all that they had stripped from the slain.
There the noble man put on fair arms, but the meaner
put on what was worse, all those whose hearts within were feeble;
but Odysseus put on what had come with him from Ithaca,
and gave to Tydeus' son Diomedes the fair arms,
those which before he had stripped from the strength of Socus;
and the son of Achilles put on his father's arms,
and seemed wholly like him; and lightly
by the hands of Hephaestus they fitted about his limbs,
though for others they were monstrous; and all together
the arms seemed light to him; nor did the helmet at all
weigh down his head, nor did the long Pelian spear
weigh heavy in his hands, but with his hands, sheer though it was,
he easily lifted it, still thirsting for blood.
And of the Argives, as many as looked upon him, could not,
though they longed to, come near, because
the heavy tumult of the war wore them down all about the wall;
as when over the wide sea, about a desert island,
far from men, shut in, men grieve
whom the squalls of the wind, blowing against them,
keep penned a very long time, and they in distress
run about the ship, and all their provisions
waste away, and at last a clear wind blows upon them as they suffer;
so the host of the Achaeans, grieving before,
rejoiced at the strength of Neoptolemus come,
hoping to breathe again from grievous toil.
And his eyes flashed like a fierce lion's,
which along the long mountains, greatly grieving in heart,
rushes against hunters, who already
climb upon his cave, eager to drag off
his cubs left alone, far from their parents,
in the shady glen; and he, from on high upon some peak,
beholding the deadly hunters, rushes upon them
roaring terribly beneath his grim jaws;
so the splendid son of fearless Aeacides
roused his spirit against the warlike Trojans;
and first he rushed where the strife most raged

title: The Fall of Troy
text:
over the plain; for there in his mind he hoped the wall of the Achaeans
was easier for the foes pressing on in the throng,
because it was built up with feebler battlements.
And with him went the others, greatly raging for Ares;
and they found strong-hearted Eurypylus, and with him his comrades
mounted upon the tower, hoping in their hearts
to break the long walls and destroy the Argives
utterly; but the gods accomplished not their desire;
but Odysseus and strong Diomedes
and godlike Neoptolemus and noble Leonteus
thrust them back from the wall with countless shafts.
And as when from the steading dogs and toiling herdsmen
with might and voice drive strong lions away,
rushing from all sides, and they with eyes gleaming gray
turn this way and that, longing greatly in their hearts
to seize calves and oxen in their jaws,
yet even so yield before the strong-hearted dogs,
driven off, for the herdsmen press hard upon them;
a little, only as far as one casts a long stone with his hand;
. . .
for Eurypylus did not let the Trojans flee away from the ships,
but very near the foes he ever urged them
to stay, until he should take the ships and destroy all
the Argives; for Zeus had cast boundless might upon him.
At once he seized a jagged and unyielding rock
and hurled it rushing against the sheer wall;
and terribly all the foundations of the lofty wall
rang round about; and fear seized all the Achaeans,
as though the wall had already crashed together in the dust.
Yet not even so did they draw back from the cruel tumult,
but remained like jackals or wolves,
shameless robbers of flocks, which in the mountains
herdsmen drive together with dogs from the caves,
eager to cast grievous slaughter upon the cubs
swiftly, while they, pressed though they are by missiles,
draw not back, but remaining defend their young;
so they, defending the ships and themselves,
remained in the battle; and bold-fighting Eurypylus
threatened them all greatly before the swift ships:
“Ah cowards, with a feeble spirit in your hearts,
you would never with your missiles have driven me back
from the ships in fear, if the wall had not warded off my war-cry;
but now you fight against me like dogs cowering before a lion
in the wood, being within, avoiding sheer slaughter;
but if ever from the ships you come out to the Trojan soil,
eager for battle as before, no one will save you
from ill-sounding death, but all together
you shall lie in the dust, slain by me.”
So he spoke, hurling an idle word; nor did he know
that a great calamity rolled upon him a little way off
by the hands of bold Neoptolemus, who was destined
to overcome him before long beneath his raging spear.
Nor even then was he without strong toil,
but he slew the Trojans from the wall; and they fled
struck from above; and they crowded round in distress
upon Eurypylus; for grievous fear seized them all;
as when little children at their father's knees
cower before the thunder of great Zeus that breaks
amid the clouds, when the air groans dreadfully;
so the sons of the Trojans among the Ceteian men
about their great king feared Neoptolemus,
and all that he cast with his hands; for straight flew the calamity,
bringing tearful Ares upon the heads of the foes.
And they, smitten within their hearts with helplessness,
the Trojans, said it was monstrous Achilles whom they beheld,
himself together with his arms; and grievous speechlessness
they hid beneath their hearts, lest dread fear should come
upon the minds of the Ceteians or of king Eurypylus;

title: The Fall of Troy
text:
and there, one here, one there, trembling boundlessly,
they stood between evil and chill terror;
for shame held them back, and grievous fear alike.
And as when men going on their feet along a rugged road
behold a torrent darting down from the mountain,
and a roar resounds about the rock,
and they no longer have heart to go down into the resounding stream
hastening, since beside their feet, beholding destruction,
they tremble and care nothing for the road;
so the Trojans remained, longing though they were to escape
. . .
the wall, before the Argives; and godlike Eurypylus
ever urged them on to the battle; for indeed he hoped
that the monstrous man, slaying many in the fight,
would tire in his hand and strength; but he ceased not from the fray.
And Athena, beholding their strong toil,
left the steep halls of fragrant Olympus,
and went over the peaks of the mountains; nor did she touch the ground
with her feet, greatly hastening; but the holy air bore her
likened to the clouds, lighter than the wind.
And quickly she reached Troy, and set her feet upon the hill
of windy Sigeum; and from there she beheld the battle-cry
of the close-fighting men, and glorified the Achaeans greatly.
And the son of Achilles held, far more than all others,
courage and strength together, which, coming together in men,
work great renown; and he excelled in both,
because he was of the blood of Zeus, and like his dear father;
therefore, fearless, he slew many near the towers.
And as a fisher on the sea, eager for his catch,
bringing destruction to the fish, carries the strength of Hephaestus
within his ship, and beneath the kindled blast
the gleam of fire shines about the ship, and they from the dark
sea dart up, eager to behold the last
brightness, for them with his long-pointed trident
he slays as they rush on, and his heart rejoices in the catch;
so the glorious son of warlike Achilles
about the stone wall overcame the hostile tribes
as they rushed against him; and all the Achaeans toiled,
some here, some at other battlements; and the wide
shore and the ships resounded, and the long walls
groaned as they were battered. And boundless weariness
overcame the host on both sides, and the limbs and strength
of the warriors were loosed; but in no way did it overcome
the godlike son of war-abiding Achilles, since his mighty heart
was wholly unwearied, and grievous fear in no way
touched him as he fought; and his might was like a tireless
ever-flowing river, which the boundless onset of fire
never, coming, frightens, even if the blast rages greatly
stirring up the holy strength of Hephaestus; for if it comes
near the mouth, it is quenched, nor has its grievous force
strength to lay hold upon the tireless water;
so for the noble son of warlike Peleus' son
neither grievous toil nor fear touched his knees
as he ever pressed on and urged on his comrades.
Nor indeed did any missile reach his fair flesh,
though many cast; but like snowflakes about a rock
often they flew in vain; for all
the broad shield warded off, and the strong helmet, glorious gifts of the god;
rejoicing in them the strong son of Aeacides
ranged about, shouting loud about the wall, often commanding
the fearless Argives to battle, because of all
he was far the best, and still had a heart insatiate
of the grievous war-cry, and devised
to avenge the grievous slaughter of his father; and the Myrmidons
rejoiced in their lord; and dread was the war-cry about the wall.
Then he slew two sons of wealthy Meges,
who was the offspring of Dymas, and had glorious sons,

title: The Fall of Troy
text:
skilled both to cast the javelin well, and well to drive the horse
in war, and skilfully to wield the long spear,
whom Periboea bore him at a single birth by the banks
of Sangarius, Celtus and Eubius; nor did they enjoy
their boundless wealth for long, because the Fates
laid upon them altogether a brief end of life;
and both, as they saw the day together, so both died
by the hands of bold Neoptolemus, the one struck
in the heart by the javelin, the other by a grievous stone
upon the head; and the strong helmet, shattered about his head,
was crushed, and confounded his brain.
And about them tribes of the foes were slain, and of others
countless; and the great work of Ares arose,
until at last the hour of unyoking came, and the ambrosial
Dawn was accomplished, and the host of fearless Eurypylus
drew back a little from the ships; and they near the towers
breathed a little; and the sons of the Trojans themselves
rested from the ill-sounding battle, because there had arisen
a grievous conflict about the wall. And now all
the Argives would have perished there beside their own ships,
had not the strong son of Achilles on that day
warded off from them the great host of the foes and Eurypylus
himself. And to him at once came near old Phoenix,
and seeing him marvelled, so like was he to the son of Peleus;
and about him came great joy and boundless grief,
grief as he remembered swift-footed Achilles,
and joy because he beheld his mighty son;
and he wept gladly, since never do the tribes of men
live without lamentation, even if at times they have joy.
And he flung himself about him, as a father would about a son
who, by the will of the gods, having endured grief a long time,
comes to his own home, a great joy to his dear father;
so he kissed the head and breast of Neoptolemus,
flinging himself about him, and in his wonder spoke this word:
“Hail to me, O noble child of Achilles, whom once I
when you were little reared in my own arms
willingly; and he by the glorious counsel of the gods
grew swiftly like a flourishing shoot; and I myself
rejoiced to look upon both his form and his valour;
and he was a great blessing to me; and equal to a son I honoured him,
a cherished son; and he, equal to his own father, honoured my heart;
for to him I was a father, and he was a son
to me in mind; you would have said, beholding us, that we were of one blood
for our oneness of heart; but in valour he was far
the greater, since in form and strength he was like the blessed ones.
To him you are wholly like; and I think that he
is still alive among the Argives; for whom sharp grief
holds me all my days, and in my grievous old age my heart
is worn; would that the heaped earth had hidden me
while he yet lived; this too is glory to a man,
to be buried by the hands of his guardian.
But, child, of him I shall not forget in my heart,
grieving; yet do not vex your spirit with sorrow;
but come, aid the Myrmidons and the horse-taming Achaeans
in their distress, greatly enraged with the foes
for your good father's sake; and you shall have noble glory
for overcoming Eurypylus, who is insatiate of battle;
for you are stronger than he, and shall be, by as much as your father
was nobler than his wretched father.”
When he had so spoken, the son of fair-haired Achilles addressed him:
“O old man, our valour in the battle
strong Fate shall decide, and overweening Ares.”
So speaking, that same day he longed to rush outside the wall
in his father's arms; but night held him back,
which, bringing to men release from toil,

title: The Fall of Troy
text:
rushed from Ocean, hiding her body in darkness.
And the sons of the Argives, as equal to strong Achilles,
honoured him beside the ships, rejoicing, because he had made them
bold by coming readily to the battle;
therefore they honoured him with glorious gifts,
giving boundless gifts, such as increase a man's wealth;
some gave gold and silver, others women
and handmaids, others boundless bronze, others iron,
others gave red wine in jars,
and swift-footed horses and the warlike arms of men
and well-made garments, the fair works of women;
and at these the dear heart of Neoptolemus was warmed.
And they busied themselves with supper at the huts,
glorifying the godlike son of Achilles
as equal to the tireless heavenly ones; and to him Agamemnon,
greatly rejoicing, spoke this word:
“Truly you are the son of bold Aeacides,
O child, since in strong might and form
and size and courage and in mind within you are like him;
therefore I greatly warm my heart for you; for indeed I hope
that by your hands and spear the hostile tribes
and the famous city of Priam will be destroyed,
because you are like your father; and I think I behold
that man beside the ships, when he raged at the Trojans
in wrath for fallen Patroclus; but he is now
among the immortals; and you the blessed ones sent forth
this day to aid the perishing Argives.”
When he had so spoken, the mighty son of Achilles addressed him:
“Would, O Agamemnon, that I had found him still alive,
that he himself might behold his dear son
in no way shaming his father's might, as I think
I shall be, if the heedless Heavenly Ones keep me safe.”
So he spoke, with his heart fitted to prudent thoughts;
and the people about him marvelled at the godlike man.
But when they had had their fill of supper and the feast,
then the mighty son of bold Aeacides
rose up from the meal and came to the hut
of his father. And there lay about him the many
arms of slain heroes; and about him, one here, one there,
the captive women set in order the widowed hut
as though their lord were living; and when he saw the arms of the Trojans
and the handmaids, he groaned; and longing for his father seized him;
as when through thick woods and bushy glens,
when a terrible lion has been overcome by hunters,
his cub comes to the shady cave, and on every side
often peers into the empty den, and there,
beholding the heaped bones of horses and oxen
slain before, not a few, greatly grieves for its sire;
so then the son of bold Peleus' son
was chilled in spirit; and the handmaids marvelled at him about him;
and Briseis herself, when she beheld the son of Achilles,
now greatly rejoiced in her heart, now again
grieved, remembering Achilles; and within her the heart
was smitten with speechlessness in her mind, as though in truth
fearless Aeacides himself were still living.
And the Trojans apart, rejoicing, glorified the mighty man
Eurypylus in their huts, they too,
as much as divine Hector, when he slew the Argives
defending his own city and all its wealth.
But when sweet sleep came upon mortals,
then the sons of the Trojans and the war-abiding Argives
apart from the watchmen slept, weighed down with sleep.
8. Now when the sunlight spread abroad over the earth,
rising from the world's edge, where the cave of the Dawn-goddess lies,
then indeed the Trojans and the mighty sons of the Achaeans
armed on either side, pressing eagerly toward the strife;
and these the noble son of Achilles urged on,
to face the Trojans with hearts that knew no fear,
and those the great might of Telephus' son drove forward; for he hoped
to cast the wall to the ground and lay the ships to ashes
in deadly fire, and cut the host down beneath his hands.
But his hope was like a wind
that comes to nothing; and the Fates, standing very near him,
laughed long at his vain devising.
And then to the Myrmidons the fearless son of Achilles
spoke a daring word, urging them on to labour:
Hear me, my comrades, and set a warlike spirit
within your breasts, that to the Argives we may be a cure for grievous war
and to our foes a ruin; let none among us
flinch; for from courage there springs valour in abundance
in men, but fear unmakes their strength
and their wits. Come now, all of you, brace yourselves for Ares,
that the Trojan host may not draw breath, but rather say
that Achilles still lives and walks among the Argives.
So speaking, he drew upon his shoulders his father's armour,
flashing from every side; and Thetis rejoiced in her heart,
gazing from the sea upon the great strength of her grandson.
And swiftly he sped out before the steep wall,
mounted upon his father's immortal horses;
and as the sun appears from the world's edge of Ocean,
flashing its fire over the wondrous earth,
fire, when together with his colts and chariot rises the star
Sirius, which brings to mortals much-grieving sickness;
so against the Trojan host went the mighty hero,
the son of Achilles; and the immortal horses bore him,
which, when he longed to drive the host back from the ships,
Automedon had given him; for he was their charioteer;
and the horses too rejoiced, bearing their lord
so like the son of Aeacus; and their deathless hearts believed
that this man was no whit less than Achilles.
So too the Argives gathered, greatly exulting,
about the strength of Neoptolemus, raging insatiably,
like deadly wasps, which when one has stirred them
. . .
they pour forth from their hole, longing to set their sting
upon human flesh, and all of them, swarming about their nest,
make great trouble for the mortals who pass by;
so these poured out from the ships and the wall,
mad for Ares; and the broad ground was crowded close.
The whole plain afar shone with the armour of men,
the sun blazing immeasurably from on high;
and as a cloud goes through the boundless air,
driven by the great gusts of Boreas,
when snowfall comes and the harsh season of winter,
and on every side the darkness crowns the sky;
so the earth was filled with these, joining battle on either hand
a little way from the ships; and dust rose
spreading into the wide heaven; and the armour of men clashed,
and with it many chariots; rushing on to the fray
the horses neighed; and each man's own valour
urged him on, summoning him to the grievous fight.
And as when two winds drive on the long waves,
roaring terribly across the broad flood of the sea,
breaking their storms against each other from afar,
when a grievous tempest rages over the wide depths of the deep,
and Amphitrite groans, unconquerable,
with her deadly waves, and they are borne, now here, now there,
like towering mountains, and from them comes a grievous
roar over the sea as they rise on either side;
so these came together for Ares from both sides,
raging terribly; and strife and valour roused them.
They clashed together like thunders or like lightnings,
which crash together through the air, when the winds
strive furiously, and when, blowing furiously,
they break the clouds together, while Zeus is greatly wroth
with men who work deeds beyond honoured Themis;
so these fell upon each other; and spear against spear
met, and shield against shield, and man went against man.
First the mighty son of warlike Achilles
slew noble Melaneus and shining Alcidamas,
the sons of wise Alexinomus, who in hollow
Caunus dwelt, near the clear-watered lake,
beneath snowy Imbros, at the foot of Tarbelus.
And he slew Menes, the swift-footed son of Cassander,
whom divine Creusa bore beside the outpourings of the river
Lindus of fair streams, where the bounds of the war-steadfast Carians
and the heights of glorious Lycia lie.
And he took the spearman Morys, who had come from Phrygia;
and with him together he slew Polybus and Hippomedon,
striking the one beneath the heart, the other at the collarbone;
and he struck down man after man; and the earth groaned with the corpses
of Trojans; and they gave way like withered
thickets that the breath of destroying fire lays low
easily as the autumn North Wind comes on;
so before his onset the battalions fell to ruin.
And Aeneas slew steadfast Aristolochus,
striking him with a stone upon the head; and he crushed
the bones together with the helmet; and at once life left the bones.
And the son of Tydeus took swift Eumaeus, who dwelt
in lofty Dardanus, where the marriage-bed of Anchises
lies, where he subdued Cytherea in his arms.
There Agamemnon slew noble Stratus; nor did he come
to Thrace again from the war, but perished far from his dear homeland.
And Meriones slew Chlemus, son of Peisenor,
the dear and trusted comrade of godlike Glaucus,
who dwelt beside the outpourings of Limyrus,
and the neighbouring men honoured him as a king,
now that Glaucus was slain and ruled no more,
all who dwelt about the seat of Phoenix
and the steep crag of Massicytus and the gorge of the Chimaera.
One man slew another through the fray; and among them
Eurypylus loosed evil dooms upon many
of his foes; and first he slew steadfast
Eurytus, and then Menoetius of the gleaming belt,
the godlike comrades of Elephenor; and beside them
Harpalus, who was the comrade of wise Odysseus;
but he had his toil far off, and could not come
to defend his servant who had fallen; and the comrade
of the slain man, strong-souled Antiphus, was wroth,
and cast straight against Eurypylus; but in no way
did he wound him, since his strong spear fell a little short
upon wise Melanion, whom once his mother
bore beside the outpourings of fair-flowing Caicus,
fair-cheeked Cleite, subdued by Erylaus.
And Eurypylus, in wrath for his slain comrade,
rushed at once upon Antiphus; but he escaped on swift feet
into the throng of his comrades; nor did the strong spear
of wise Telephus' son destroy him, since he was fated
to perish wretchedly beneath the man-slaying Cyclops
later; so it pleased hateful Fate.
And Eurypylus went raging on the other side; and beneath his spear,
as ever he pressed on, a great crowd fell;
as when tall trees, brought low by the force of iron
in shaggy mountains, fill the ravines,
laid this way and that upon the ground; so the Achaeans
were laid low by the spears of wise Eurypylus,
until against him came, high-minded in his heart,
the son of Achilles. And both their long spears
they shook in their hands, raging against each other;
and Eurypylus first questioned him and spoke:
Who are you, and whence have you come to fight against us?
Surely the pitiless Fates are bearing you to Hades;
for no man has escaped me in grievous battle;
but all who came hither, eager to fight
against me, on all of them I sent grievous slaughter
cruelly, and beside the streams of Xanthus
the dogs have shared out among them all the bones and flesh.
But tell me, who are you, in what horses do you glory?
So he spoke, and the mighty son of Achilles answered him:
Why, as I press on to the bloody fray,
being my enemy, do you ask as though in friendship
that I tell my lineage, which very many know?
I am the son of strong-souled Achilles, who once
put your father to flight, striking him with his long spear;
and the evil Fates of death would then have seized him,
had not your father swiftly healed his grievous wound.
The horses that bear me are my godlike father's,
which the Harpy bore after lying once with Zephyrus,
who run across even the barren sea with their feet,
touching it with their hooves' tips, and are borne swift as the winds.
Now, since you have learned the lineage of the horses and of myself,
make trial too of our unwearied spear,
and know its force in close fight; for its lineage is on the heights
of steep Pelion, where it left the cleft stump and the wood.
So he spoke, and the glorious man leapt from his horses to the ground,
brandishing his enormous spear; and the other from his side
seized in his strong hands a boundless stone,
and hurled it to strike the golden shield
of Neoptolemus. But, for all its onset, it did not stagger him,
but he stood like a vast headland upon a great mountain,
which the might of the heaven-fed rivers, not even all of them together,
can thrust back, for it is rooted firm;
so the mighty son of Achilles stood ever unflinching.
Yet even so the bold strength of Eurypylus was not afraid
of the irresistible son of Achilles, since his own courage
and the Fates urged him on; and the spirit beneath their hearts
boiled in them both; and about them their gleaming armour
rang; and like wild beasts they came upon each other,
terrible, beasts whose strife grows fierce among the mountains,
when, stricken in heart by grievous hunger,
they toil over a slain ox or stag,
both raging, and the glens echo
as they fight; so these came together against each other,
joining a relentless strife. And on either side
the long battalions of the host toiled wearily about them
into the fray; and grievous strife arose about them.
And they, like the swift rushings of the winds,
clashed together with their ashen spears, eager to spill
each other's blood; and ever Enyo urged them on,
standing near at hand; and they did not cease from the war-cry,
but kept hewing at each other's shields, and now again
struck the greaves and the high-crested helmets;
and at times one even touched the flesh, for grievous toil pressed
the bold heroes hard; and Strife took delight in her heart,
gazing upon them; and much sweat poured down
from both; and ever they braced themselves, holding their ground;
for both were of the blood of the blessed; and from Olympus—
. . .
For some gave glory to the mighty son of Achilles,
and others to godlike Eurypylus; and on either side
they fought, like unwearied crags
of towering mountains; and loudly on both sides rang
their shields, struck again and again by ashen spears; and at last the long
Pelian spear passed through the throat of Eurypylus,
after much toil; and his dark blood gushed out
in a stream; and his soul flew out through the wound
from his limbs, and a deadly darkness fell upon his eyes.
And he fell in his armour to the ground, like a tall
pine or fir uprooted from its roots
by the force of the chill North Wind; so great a stretch of earth
the body of Eurypylus covered; and loudly groaned the Trojan ground
and the plain. And swiftly upon the corpse
a pale hue was poured, and dimmed its fair flush.
And exulting over him the strong hero greatly boasted:
Eurypylus, surely you said you would ravage the ships of the Danaans,
and us ourselves, and destroy us all
wretchedly; but the gods did not fulfil your wish for you,
but beneath my hand, unwearied though it was,
my father's great spear has subdued you, the spear which no mortal shall escape
who comes against me, not even were he all of bronze.
So he spoke, and drew the enormous spear-point from the corpse
swiftly; and the Trojans greatly trembled, beholding
the strong-hearted man; and at once, stripping off the armour,
he gave it to his swift comrades to bear to the ships of the Achaeans;
and he himself, leaping into the swift chariot and behind the unwearied horses,
went on, like the thunderbolt that goes through the boundless air
from tireless Zeus, together with the lightning-flashes,
which even the immortals dread as it comes down,
all but great Zeus, and it, rushing toward the earth,
shatters trees and the rugged mountains;
so swiftly he rushed on the Trojans, arming ruin against them;
and he struck down one here, one there, all whom the immortal horses overtook;
and the ground was filled, and reddened deep with gore.
And as when countless leaves over the glens of a mountain
lie thickly fallen, strewn over the wide earth;
so the host of the Trojans then, past counting, lay upon the ground
beneath the hands of Neoptolemus and the high-souled Argives,
beneath whose hands streamed dark blood unspeakable
of men and horses; and the rims about the chariots,
turning, were drenched amid their own whirling tracks.
And now the sons of Troy would have come within the gates,
like calves fleeing a lion or swine fleeing a storm,
had not grievous Ares, longing to bring aid
to the war-loving Trojans, come down from Olympus
secretly from the other blessed ones; and the horses bore him to the fray,
Aithon and Phlogios, and after them Konabos and Phobos,
whom for loud-roaring Boreas the grim-eyed Erinys bore,
breathing destroying fire; and the gleaming air groaned beneath them
as they sped to the strife. And swiftly he came
to Troy; and beneath him the earth resounded greatly under the dread
hooves of his horses; and coming near the tumult of battle
he brandished his heavy spear; and loudly he cried, urging the Trojans
to face their foes through the fray; and they, hearing
the wondrous voice, all marvelled; for they did not see
the immortal body of the deathless god, nor his horses;
for he was hidden in mist. But the divine voice
the glorious mind of godlike Helenus marked,
darting from somewhere full upon the ears of the Trojans;
and in his heart he rejoiced, and loudly called to the fleeing host:
Ah cowards, why do you flee the bold son
of war-loving Achilles? He too is some mortal man,
nor is his strength equal to Ares, who greatly aids
us in our longing; he calls aloud, urging at length
that we fight the Argives through the fray; come then, my friends,
endure in your hearts, and cast courage into your breasts;
for I think no better defender against war
will come to the Trojans; for what in the strife of Ares
is better, when he aids mortals as they arm for battle?
And he has now come to us as a helper; come, you too
remember battle, and cast fear far away.
So he spoke; and they stood facing the Argives;
as when in the thickets dogs, against a wolf
fleeing before, turn their strength to fight,
when the shepherd ever urges them on with words;
so the sons of Troy in the dread strife of Ares
were beyond fear; and man fought against man
boldly; and about them rang the gear of warriors,
struck by swords and spears and arrows;
and the spear-points sank into flesh; and dread Ares
was drenched with much blood; and they perished in the fray, one upon another,
as they fought on either side; and the battle held even balance.
And as when strong men along the slope of a great vineyard
cut through the rows of vines with iron,
hastening, and the work of each grows equal in their rivalry,
since they are equal in age and in strength;
so on both sides the grievous scales of battle
were even; for the Trojans, setting overweening hearts within,
held their ground, trusting in the valour of fearless Ares;
and the Argives trusted in the son of war-steadfast Achilles.
And they kept slaying each other; and deadly Enyo
ranged through the midst, her shoulders spattered with grievous gore,
and her hands; and from her limbs ran dread sweat;
nor did she defend either side, but delighted in the equal battle,
honouring in her heart Thetis and divine Ares.
There Neoptolemus slew far-famed Perimedes,
who had his house beside the Sminthian grove;
and after him he slew Cestrus and steadfast Phalerus
and strong Perilaus and Menalces of the good ashen spear,
whom Iphianassa bore beside the sacred foot of Cilla
to skilled Medon, knowing in the craft of building;
but he remained at home in his dear native land,
and had no joy of his son; and his house and all his works
the next of kin, after he had perished, divided among themselves.
And Deiphobus slew steadfast Lycon,
striking him a little above the groin; and about the long spear
all his entrails poured out; and his whole belly burst forth.
And Aeneas slew Dymas, who once before
dwelt in Aulis, and had followed Arcesilaus
to Troy; but never again did he look upon his dear land.
And Euryalus slew, casting a grievous javelin,
Astraeus; and at once through his breast flew
the painful spear-point, and cut away the passages of his gullet,
bringing doom to the man; and his food was mingled with gore.
And a little way off high-souled Agenor took
Hippomenes, the noble comrade of wise Teucer,
striking him swiftly at the collarbone; and with his blood his spirit
leapt from his limbs; and deadly night was poured about him.
And grief fell on Teucer for his slain comrade,
and he cast a swift arrow, drawing it straight against Agenor;
but in no way did he hit him, for he swerved a very little;
but it fell upon wise Deiophontes, who stood near,
into his left eye, and through his right ear it passed,
and clove the eyeball, since the Fates
drove the grievous shaft where they would; and still upon his feet
he stood and started up; but casting a second shaft
. . .
he made it whistle at his throat; and it cut through the sinews of the neck,
darting straight on; and grievous Fate overtook him.
One man wrought death upon another; and the Fates rejoiced
and Doom, and grievous Strife, raging greatly,
shouted very loud, and Ares answered her
terribly, and breathed great courage into the Trojans,
but into the Argives flight, and at once he shook their battalions.
Yet he did not put to flight the son of Achilles; but he, standing fast,
fought boldly, and slew one after another;
and as when a young boy, against the flies that come
about the milk, flings his hand round, and they beneath the blow,
even a slight one, are killed near the vessel, this way and that,
and breathe out their life, and the child delights in the work;
so the glorious son of relentless Achilles
rejoiced about the corpses, and took no heed of Ares
urging on the Trojans; and he punished one here, one there,
as the host rushed on; and as the crest of a great mountain
abides the storms of the wind that rush upon it,
so he abode unflinching. And Ares, in his raging,
was wroth with him, and was minded to fight against him
in his own person, casting off the holy cloud, had not Athena
darted from somewhere out of Olympus to shadowy Ida;
and the divine earth trembled, and the echoing streams
of Xanthus; so greatly she shook it; and fear broke the hearts
of the nymphs, and they feared for the city of Priam;
and about her immortal armour the lightnings flew;
and terrible serpents from her unwearied shield
breathed unceasing fire; and her wondrous helmet
touched the clouds on high. And she was about to fight swiftly
against eager Ares, had not the good purpose of Zeus
frightened them both away, thundering grievously
from the steep heaven. And Ares drew back from the battle;
for the wrath of great Zeus was made plain to him;
and he went off to wintry Thrace, and no longer
cared in his overweening heart for the Trojans; nor did noble
Pallas remain any more on the Trojan plain, but she too
went to the holy ground of the Athenians. And the others still
were minded for the deadly strife; but the sons of Troy
lacked valour; and the Argives, greatly straining toward war,
followed close on the heels of those who gave way, like winds
upon ships rushing under sail into the great swell of the sea,
mighty, or like the force of fire upon thickets, or like
keen hounds upon young deer along the mountains, hot for the chase;
so the Danaans came on against their foes, since the son
of Achilles heartened them with his great spear,
slaying whomever he overtook through the fray; and they, in flight,
giving way, plunged down into the high-gated city.
And the Argives breathed a little from the war,
having penned the tribes of the Trojans within the city of Priam,
as shepherds pen lambs in lonely folds;
and as when oxen, greatly wearied, take breath,
having dragged a load up to a hard-climbed height,
panting thick beneath the yoke; so the Achaeans
took breath in their armour, wearied. And about the towers,
eager to fight, they encircled the city;
and the Trojans, drawing the bolts upon their gates,
waited within the walls for the onset of the raging men.
And as when shepherds remain within their folds
against the dark squall, when the day of winter comes,
furious, with lightning and rain and snow
thick-falling, and they, however much they long to go
to pasture, do not rush forth, until the great storm
abates and the broad-flowing rivers, loudly roaring;
so these remained within the walls, dreading the war-cry
of their foes; and the host swiftly poured against the city.
And as when long-winged starlings or jackdaws
fall in throngs upon the olive's fruit,
eager for the sweet food, and the young men,
shouting, do not turn them to flight
before they have fed, for hunger swells their shameless heart;
so the Danaans then poured about the city of Priam,
mighty; and they fell upon the gates, eager to drag down
the boundless work of the strong-hearted Earth-shaker.
But the Trojans did not forget battle, though greatly afraid,
but even so, standing upon the towers, they toiled
unceasingly; and arrows ever from the well-built walls
leapt, together with stones and swift javelins,
into the throng of their foes, since Phoebus
had put steadfast strength in them; for his heart still wished
to defend the war-skilled Trojans, even though Hector was gone.
There Meriones sent forth a hateful shaft
and struck Phylodamas, dear son of strong Polites,
a little beneath the jaw; and the arrow stuck beneath his throat.
And he fell like a vulture, which from a rock
a young man strikes with a barbed shaft and slays;
so swiftly he fell from the steep tower;
and his spirit left his limbs; and his armour rang upon the corpse.
And exulting over him the son of strong Molus
loosed another arrow, longing greatly in his heart
to strike the son of much-enduring Priam, Polites;
but he swiftly avoided it, bending aside
his body, and the shaft did not wound his fair flesh;
and as when over the depth of the sea, with the ship hastening before the wind,
a sailor, seeing a rugged rock amid the flood,
turns the ship aside, eager to escape it,
bending the steering-oar with his hand, where his heart
urges him, and a small effort wards off great harm;
so he, seeing the deadly shaft before it came, escaped his doom.
And ever they fought; and the walls grew red with gore,
the high towers and the battlements, where the Trojans
were slain by arrows beneath the strong Achaeans;
nor were these themselves free from toil, but of them too
many reddened the earth; and steep destruction arose
as they were struck on either side; and baleful Enyo took delight,
driving on the strife, the sister of War.
And now the Argives would have broken the gates and walls of Troy,
for their strength was unspeakably great,
had not glorious Ganymede at once cried out,
looking down from heaven; for he greatly feared for his fatherland:
Father Zeus, if in truth I am of your stock,
and by your counsels, leaving glorious Troy,
am among the immortals, and my life is deathless,
then hear me now, sorely grieved at heart:
for I shall not endure to look upon the city burning,
nor upon my race perishing in the grievous
slaughter, than which there is no worse pain;
but if your heart is set on devising these things,
do them apart from me; lighter shall be my grief,
if I do not see it with my own eyes;
for that is most piteous and most shameful, when one
sees his fatherland laid waste by the hands of foes.
So spoke the shining heart of Ganymede, groaning deeply.
And then Zeus himself with boundless clouds
unceasingly covered the famed city of Priam;
and the man-destroying battle was darkened; nor was any man
able any more to see the wall, where it was built;
for it was covered continuously with thick clouds;
and round about thunders and lightnings crashed
from heaven. And the Danaans, hearing the thunder of Zeus,
marvelled; and among them the son of Neleus loudly cried:
O glorious leaders of the Argives, no longer
will our limbs be steadfast, since Zeus greatly aids
the bold Trojans; for he rolls a great calamity
upon us; come then, more quickly going to our ships,
let us cease from toil and grievous battle,
lest he burn us all, raging though greatly we strive.
Now let us yield to his portents; for it is fitting
that all should ever yield to him, since he is far the best
of the mighty gods and of feeble men;
for when, wroth with the overweening Titans,
he poured down from heaven the force of fire; and below
the earth burned on every side, and the broad flood of Ocean
boiled from its depths, even to its furthest bounds;
and the streams of the long-flowing rivers were dried;
and he subdued whatever tribes the life-giving earth nourished,
and whatever the boundless sea fed, and whatever the water
of the ever-flowing rivers; and over them the boundless air
was hidden in ash and smoke; and the earth was worn away;
therefore I fear the might of Zeus on this day.
But let us go to the ships, since today he aids the Trojans;
yet afterward he will grant glory to us also;
for at one time the dawn is friendly, at another hostile;
and it is not yet fated that the famed city be sacked,
if the word of Calchas was truly spoken,
which he once declared to the assembled Achaeans,
that we should sack the city of Priam in the tenth year.
So he spoke; and they, leaving the glorious city afar,
drew back from the war, dreading the war-cry of Zeus;
for they obeyed a man skilled in the lore of old.
Yet even so they did not neglect those slain in battle,
but buried them, drawing them out of the war;
for the cloud did not cover those, but the lofty
city and the unscalable wall, about which many
sons of the Trojans and of the Argives were slain by Ares.
And coming to the ships they laid aside their warlike gear,
and washed off the dust and sweat and gore,
plunging into the waves of the fair-flowing Hellespont.
And the Sun drove his unwearied horses down beneath the gloom;
and night was poured about the earth, and turned men from their labours;
and the Argives honoured the bold son of war-skilled Achilles
like his own father; and he in the huts of the chiefs
feasted, exulting; and no weariness weighed him down,
since Thetis had taken from his limbs the grievous
cares, and made him to look upon like one untired;
and he, when he had satisfied his strong heart with food,
came to the hut of his father, where sleep
was poured about him; and the Danaans before the ships lay
ever changing their watches; for they feared greatly
lest the host of the Trojans or of their close-fighting allies
should burn the ships and rob them all of their return.
And likewise throughout the city of Priam the tribes of the Trojans
about the gates and the wall slept by turns,
dreading the grievous war-cry of the Argives.

title: The Fall of Troy
text:
9. Now when the darkness was spent from the night, and Dawn awoke
from the world's edge, and the boundless air shone immeasurable,
then the warlike sons of the strong Argives
gazed over the plain, and saw the height of Ilium
cloudless; and they marvelled greatly at yesterday's great portent.
But the Trojans no longer thought to stand before the steep wall
in war; for great fear had seized them all,
believing that the glorious son of Peleus still lived;
and Antenor among them prayed to the lord of the gods:
Zeus, ruler of Ida and of the gleaming heaven,
hear me as I pray, and turn the mighty man from our city,
the man who devises ruin in his heart,
whether he be Achilles and has not gone to the house of Hades,
or some other Achaean like to that man;
for the people throughout the city of god-born Priam
perish in numbers, and there is no respite from evil,
but slaughter and doom ever increase the more;
Father Zeus, do you take no thought at all for those cut down by the Achaeans,
but you too, forgetful of your own son,
godlike Dardanus, greatly aid the Argives.
But if your heart longs for this within your breast,
to destroy the Trojans wretchedly beneath the Argives,
do it at once, and do not make our griefs last long.
So he prayed greatly; and Zeus heard him from heaven;
and the one thing he fulfilled at once, but the other he was not to fulfil;
for he nodded that many of the Trojans should perish
together with their children, but the wise son of Achilles
he did not nod to turn away from the spacious city,
but rather roused him the more, since now his heart bade him
bring favour and glory to the kindly daughter of Nereus.
So pondered he who is far the greatest of the other gods.
And between the city and the wide Hellespont
the Argives and Trojans were burning those slain in battle
together with their horses; and the fight had ceased from slaughter,
because the might of Priam had sent the herald Menoetes
to Agamemnon and all the other Achaeans,
entreating them to burn the dead with fire; and they consented,
out of reverence for the slain; for no wrath attends the dead.
And when they had made many pyres for the fallen,
then the Argives came back to their huts,
and the Trojans to the halls of Priam rich in gold,
grieving very much for fallen Eurypylus;
for they had honoured him equal to Priam's own children;
therefore they buried him apart from the other slain
before the Dardanian gate, where the long stream
. . .
of the eddying river pours on, swollen by the rain of Zeus.
And the son of fearless Achilles came to his father's
moss-grown tomb; and weeping he kissed
the well-wrought pillar of his dead father;
and groaning he spoke this word:
Hail, father, even beneath the earth below; for I
shall not forget you, gone to the house of Hades;
would that I had found you alive among the Argives;
then quickly, taking joy in each other in our hearts,
we should have plundered from sacred Ilium its untold wealth;
but now neither did you see your child, nor did I
see you alive, though I longed to behold you.
Yet even so, though you are gone and among the dead,
your spear and your son the enemy greatly shudder at in battle,
and the Danaans behold him with joy,
so like to you in body and stature and in deeds.
So speaking, he wiped the warm tear from his cheeks.
And swiftly he went to the ships of his high-souled father,
not alone; for with him went twelve men
of the Myrmidons, and the old man Phoenix followed among them,
mournfully groaning for glorious Achilles.
And night came over the earth, and the stars rushed up to heaven;
and they, having supped, took sleep; and Dawn awoke.
And the Argives put on their armour; and far from them
a gleam flashed, going up to the sky;
and swiftly they rushed forth outside the gates,
all together, like snowflakes, which fall
thick from the clouds in the chill season of winter;
so they poured out before the wall, and a cry arose,
terrible; and the great earth groaned about them as they came.
And the Trojans, when they heard the shout and saw the host,
were amazed; and the heart within them all was broken,
foreboding their doom; for like a cloud appeared
the host of their foes; and the armour of the men clanged
as they moved; and the dust rose unceasing beneath their feet.
And then either some god cast courage within the heart
of Deiphobus and made him very fearless, or his own
spirit urged him to the fray, that from his fatherland
he might drive the grievous host of foes beneath his spear;
and he spoke a bold word among the Trojans:
O friends, come now, set a warlike spirit within your breasts,
remembering how many griefs the end of grievous war
brings upon men taken captive by the spear;
for the contest is not for Alexander alone,
nor for Helen, but it is for our city and for ourselves
and for our wives and dear children and honoured parents
and all our splendour and our wealth and our lovely
land, which I would rather have cover me, slain in the fray,
than that I should behold my dear fatherland beneath the spears
of foes; for I think there is no worse other
calamity wrought among wretched men.
Therefore, all of you, thrusting hateful fear from around me,
brace yourselves for the relentless strife; for Achilles
no longer lives to fight against us, since
the deadly fire devoured him; and there is some other of the Achaeans
who now rouses the host; and it is fitting that neither Achilles
nor any other Achaean we should dread, when fighting
for our fatherland; therefore let us not flee the toil of Ares,
even if before this we have endured much in our suffering.
Or do you not yet know this in your hearts, how to long-suffering
men out of toil come feasting and prosperity,
and out of grievous winds and dread winter
Zeus brings to mortals through the air a fair-weather day,
and out of deadly sickness comes strength, and out of battle
peace? All these works are changed by time.
So he spoke; and they, raging for Ares, made themselves ready
hastily; and a clamour arose throughout the city everywhere,
as the young men armed for the grievous fray.
There for one his wife, trembling at the tumult,
brought his armour as he went off, shedding tears;
and for another his little sons, hurrying about their father,
bore all his gear; and he at one moment
grieved with them as they mourned, but at another smiled in turn,
glorying in his sons; and his heart in battle the more
was eager to toil for his children and for himself;
and for another the old father with skilled hands
set about his limbs the defences against the evil fray,
greatly cheering his dear son not to yield to any
in war, and showed his battered breast to his child,
bearing many marks of an old fighting.
But when at last they were all armed in their gear,
they poured out of the city, greatly longing for war,
the grievous war; and upon swift horsemen rushed
the horsemen; and upon footmen the tribes of footmen fell;
and chariots came against chariots; and the earth resounded
as they sped to the fray; and each shouted to his own,
calling on them; and at once they joined battle; and about them
the armour clashed; and from both sides was mingled the cry,
grievous; and many shafts swiftly flew,
hurled from both sides; and beneath the spears the shields of men,
struck, rang unbearably; and others beneath javelins
and swords; and many men were wounded too
by swift axes; and the gear of the warriors was fouled
with blood. And the Trojan women watched from the wall
the grievous strife of the young men; and the limbs of them all
trembled as they prayed for their children and their husbands
and their brothers; and along with them the grey-haired old men
sat watching; and their hearts were eaten with anxiety
for their dear sons; and Helen remained in the halls
alone with her handmaids; for unspeakable shame held her back.
And they toiled ceaselessly before the wall; and about them the Fates
rejoiced; and baleful Strife, shouting long, urged on
both sides with her cry; and the dust grew red with gore
of the slain; and they perished through the fray, one here, one there.
There Deiphobus slew the strong charioteer
of Nestor, the son of Hippasus; and he from the swift chariot
fell among the corpses; and grief seized his lord;
for he feared lest, while his hands were on the reins,
the noble son of Priam should slay him too;
but Melanthius did not fail him; for upon the chariot
he leapt swiftly, and called to the horses, shaking the long
reins, and held no whip, but drove, striking with his spear.
And the son of Priam left them, and came to the throng
of others; and to many he gave a deadly day,
hastening; for like a deadly storm ever
he fell boldly upon his foes; and beneath his hands
men past counting were slain; and the plain was crowded with corpses.
And as when one springs along the great mountains into the hollows of a glen,
a woodcutter, hurrying, lays low the freshly-flourishing wood,
that he may burn charcoal, hiding beneath the earth
with fire much timber; and it, falling this way and that,
covers the headlands above, and the man takes joy in the work;
so beneath the swift hands of Deiphobus the Achaeans,
slain in droves, fell about one another.
And some closed with the Trojans, and others fled
to the wide stream of Xanthus; and into the water
Deiphobus drove them, and did not cease from slaughter;
and as when on the shores of the fish-filled Hellespont
much-toiling fishermen draw out a net,
bellied toward the land, and while it is still within the sea
a young man leaps in, grasping a bent spear in his hands,
to bring dread slaughter upon the swordfish, and one here, one there
he lays low, whomever he overtakes, and the water grows red with slaughter;
so beneath his hands about the streams of Xanthus
the waters were reddened with blood, and crowded with corpses.
Nor indeed did the Trojans toil without bloodshed,
but the mighty son of Achilles cut them down
among the other battalions; and Thetis, watching,
took joy in her grandson, as much as she had grieved for the son of Peleus;
for beneath his ashen spear a great host in the dust
fell together with the horses; and he, following, made havoc.
There he slew far-famed Amides, who, seated upon his horse,
met with him, and had no joy of his lovely
horsemanship; for he struck him with his shining spear
in the belly, and the point passed through to his back;
and his entrails poured out; and deadly Doom seized him
swiftly, fallen beside the feet of the swift horse.
And he took Ascanius and Oenops, driving the one
with his spear through the gullet to the mouth, the other beneath the throat,
where most of all death comes mortally to men.
And he slew others ever, all whom he overtook; who could tell
of those men, how many perished in the fray
beneath the hands of Neoptolemus? for never did his hand grow weary;
and as when one of the young men in a flourishing field
all day long, toiling with strong hands,
pours down to the earth the boundless fruit of the olive,
driving it with his rod, and covers the ground above;
so beneath his hands the great throng fell down.
And the son of Tydeus on the other side, and Agamemnon of the good ashen spear,
and others among the Danaans, the chiefs, toiled
eagerly through the relentless strife; nor among the noble
leaders of the Trojans was there fear, but they too
fought from the heart, and ever held back the men
who gave way; yet many, heedless of their lords,
fled from the war, dreading the might of the Achaeans.
And at last he marked, about the outpourings of Scamander,
the Danaans perishing, the strong son of Aeacus' son,
ever in greater numbers; he left those whom before he was slaying there,
fleeing toward the city, and bade Automedon
drive there, where the great host of the Achaeans was being slain.
And he obeyed at once, and with the whip drove on the might
of the immortal horses toward the fray; and they flew
swiftly through the slain, bearing their strong lord.
And as Ares goes alone into man-destroying war,
mounted upon his horses, and the earth trembles
as he rushes on, and about the god's breast his divine
armour rings, flashing like fire;
such was the son of strong Achilles as he went against
noble Deiphobus; and much dust rose up
about the horses' feet; and the valiant man,
Automedon, saw and knew who it was; and at once to his lord
he spoke this word, declaring the glorious man:
O lord, this is the host of Deiphobus, who himself
once before trembled at your father; but now some noble
god or spirit has cast courage beneath his heart.
So he spoke; but the other answered nothing, but still more
urged the horses to be driven, that as quickly as possible
he might ward off unseemly doom from the perishing Danaans.
But when at last they came very near to each other,
then Deiphobus, though greatly longing for war,
stood still, like dread fire when it comes near to water;
and he marvelled, beholding the horses of the strong-hearted son of Aeacus,
and the gigantic son, in no way less than his father.
And his heart within his breast pondered
now to flee, now to fight against the man face to face;
and as when in the mountains a boar from her newborn young
drives off the jackals, and a lion appears on the other side,
rushing from somewhere, and the boar's boundless rush is stayed,
neither eager to go forward any more nor backward,
and she whets her foaming teeth beneath her jaws;
so the son of Priam stayed with chariot and horses,
much troubled in his heart, and fingering the spear in his hands.
And the son of relentless Achilles spoke to him:
Son of Priam, why now do you rage so against the Argives,
the weaker men, who, dreading your war-cry,
fled as you rushed on, while you fancied yourself by far the best?
But if there is might beneath your heart,
make trial of our irresistible spear amid the fray.
So speaking, he sprang on like a lion against a stag,
mounted upon his father's horses and chariot;
and now he would quickly have slain him with the spear, charioteer and all,
had not Apollo at once poured a dark cloud about him
from somewhere out of Olympus, and from the deadly fray
snatched him away, and set him within the city, where the other
Trojans were going in flight; and he, striking the empty
air with his spear, the son of Peleus spoke this word:
O dog, you have escaped my might; nor did your own valour,
for all your eagerness, defend you, but some god, who hid you,
casting night above, and drew you out of disaster.
So he spoke; and the dark cloud above the son of Cronos
straightway dispersed like mist; and it melted into the wide air;
and at once appeared the plain and all the earth about.
And he saw the Trojans, being far off,
about the Scaean gates; and he went, like his father,
against the foe, who dreaded him as he came;
as when sailors dread a grievous wave rushing on,
which, roused by the wind, is borne
very wide and high, and the sea rages with the squall;
so an evil fear seized the Trojans as he came on.
And he spoke this word, urging on his comrades:
Hear, friends, and cast courage into your breasts,
fearless, such as it befits brave men to bear,
longing to win glorious victory with their hands
and renown from grievous war; come then, with hearts
set firm, let us toil beyond our strength, until we sack
the famed city of Troy and fulfil our desire;
for it is a shame, remaining here a very long time,
to be without achievement and feeble, like women;
for I would rather die than be called no warrior.
So he spoke; and they rushed still more to the work of Ares
boldly, and ran upon the Trojans; and these too
fought eagerly about the city, and at another time
from within the gates from the wall; nor did dread
Ares cease, the Trojans longing to drive off
the dread host of foes, and the strong Argives
to lay waste the city; and deadly misery held them all.
And then, longing to bring aid to the Trojans,
the son of Leto darted from Olympus, veiled in clouds;
and at once swift gusts bore him,
adorned in golden armour; and about him the long
paths gleamed like lightning as he came down;
and about him his quiver clashed; and the air resounded
wondrously, and the earth cried out greatly, when he set his unwearied
feet beside the stream of Xanthus; and he shouted out
terribly, and cast boldness into the Trojans, but fear into the Achaeans,
to stand fast in the bloody fray. Nor did the mighty Earth-shaker
fail to know it; and he breathed might into the Achaeans,
already hard pressed; and a destroying battle was made
by the will of the immortals; and countless tribes
of the young men perished on both sides. And Apollo, in his wrath
against the Argives, was minded to strike the bold son of Achilles
there, where before he had struck Achilles; but his heart
the birds held back, crying on the left,
and many other signs; and his wrath was no longer
willing to obey the portents; but it did not escape the Dark-haired one;
. . .
veiled in wondrous mist; and about the feet
of the lord as he came on the dark earth was stirred;
and he spoke this word, longing to restrain him:
Stay your wrath, and do not in any way slay the gigantic son
of Achilles; for not even the Olympian himself, were he slain,
will rejoice; and great grief will be to me and to all
the gods of the sea, as before for Achilles;
but draw back to the divine air, lest you anger me,
and at once, breaking open a deep chasm of the great earth,
Ilium itself, with all its walls,
I shall set straightway beneath the wide gloom; and grief will be to you yourself.
So he spoke; and the other, greatly revering the brother of his own father,
and fearing for the city and for the strong people at once,
drew back to the wide heaven, and Poseidon to the sea. And they fought,
slaying one another, and Strife took delight in the battle,
until at last, by the counsels of Calchas, the Achaeans
drew back to their ships and forgot the fray;
for it was not fated that the city of Ilium be subdued,
before the strength of Philoctetes should come to the host of the Achaeans,
skilled in tearful war.
And this either he learned from the good birds,
or he had seen it in the entrails; for not ignorant
of prophecy was he; like a god he knew all things.
Trusting in him, withdrawing from the grievous war,
the sons of Atreus sent forth to well-built Lemnos
the mighty son of Tydeus and war-steadfast Odysseus
in a swift ship; and at once to the city of Hephaestus
they came through the broad flood of the Aegean sea,
to vine-clad Lemnos, where once dread destruction
the women devised for their wedded husbands,
fiercely wroth, since they no longer honoured them,
but lay beside slave women,
Thracian women, whom by the spear and their manhood they had won
when once they sacked the land of the war-loving Thracians;
and the women, with great jealousy fallen upon their hearts,
swelled with fury in their spirit, and the dear husbands throughout their halls
they slew pitilessly, beneath their hands, nor did they pity them,
wedded though they were; for greatly does the heart rage
of man and of woman, when with a jealous sickness
it is stricken; for strong anguish urges it on;
but they cast ruin upon their own husbands
in a single night, and widowed the whole city,
setting in their breasts a fearless heart and great strength.
And when they came to sacred Lemnos and to the cave
of stone, where lay the son of glorious Poeas,
then amazement came upon them, when they beheld
the man groaning over his grievous pains,
laid upon the harsh ground; and about him
many feathers of birds were strewn about his bed;
and others were sewn together about his body, a defence against the grievous
winter; for whenever joyless hunger seized him,
he loosed an irresistible shaft, where his mind directed;
and some of these he devoured, and with the feathers he wrapped himself.
And leaves lay beside him, which
over his deadly wound
he set above as a defence against black anguish.
And his hair lay matted about his head
like a deadly beast, whom the snare of a grievous hunt
catches as it goes by night on swift foot, and it, under constraint,
in its distress, with cruel teeth gnaws off the tip
of its foot, and comes to its own cave, and about its heart
hunger together wears it and grievous cares;
so beneath the wide cave an evil anguish wasted him utterly;
and all his body was withered, and about his bones was only
skin, and a deadly squalor lay over his cheeks
as he wallowed wretchedly; and grievous pain
subdued him; and hollow beneath his brows were the man's eyes
as he was sorely worn; and lamentation never left him,
because his black wound, reaching even to the bone,
festering above, the grievous anguish ate away beneath.
And as when on the headlands of the much-washed sea
the brine of the boundless deep wears down
a rugged rock, cutting it from below, though it be very hard,
and as it is struck by wind and furious storm
hollows are scooped, eaten away by the sea;
so the wound on his foot grew greater as it festered
from the shaft, which the deadly water-snake had pressed into him
with its cruel teeth, the snake which they say is incurable and hateful,
when the strength of the sun dries it as it goes along the dry land;
so it wore down the greatest of men,
subdued by pains hard to heal;
and from his wound, ever flowing to the ground,
the ichor spattered the floor of the spacious cave,
a great wonder to men and to those who should come after.
And beside his couch leaned a long quiver
full of arrows; and some were for the hunt,
and others for his foes, which the deadly venom of the snake
of dread doom encompassed; and before him his great bow
lay near, fitted with bent horns,
wrought by the unwearied hands of Heracles.
And when he saw them coming to the wide cave,
he sprang up hastily to draw against them both
his grievous shafts, remembering his dread wrath,
because before they had left him, groaning greatly,
alone on the desolate shores of the sea.
And now he would quickly have done what his bold heart wished,
had not Athena dispersed his grievous wrath
as he gazed at the men, his comrades; and they near him
came, like men in grief; and both of them,
sitting beside him on either side within the hollow cave,
asked him about his deadly wound and his grievous pains;
and he told them his anguish.
And they cheered him; and they said that his grievous wound
they would heal of its deadly trouble and pain,
if he came to the Achaean host, which they said
was itself greatly troubled beside the ships, and the sons of Atreus
themselves along with them; and they said that none of the Achaeans
in the host was to blame for his ills, but the grievous
Fates, far from whom no man walks the earth,
but ever, unseen, over wretched men
they move all their days, harming the race of mortals at one time
in their relentless heart, and at another time
glorifying them from afar; for all things for mortals
those Fates contrive, both grievous and gentle,
just as they themselves will. And he, hearing Odysseus
and godlike Diomedes, at once his spirit
easily ceased from its grievous wrath,
fiercely wroth before for all that he had suffered.
And they quickly to the ship and the loud-thundering shores
exulting bore him together with his shafts;
and they washed his body and his relentless wound
with a well-pierced sponge, and bathed it with much water.
And he revived a little; and at once, hastening,
they made him a good meal, eager though he was; and they too
feasted within the ship. And ambrosial night came on,
and sleep rushed upon them; and they remained until the Dawn-goddess
by the shores of sea-girt Lemnos; but with the dawn
they raised the cables together with the well-bent anchor-stones
from outside, hastening; and Athena sent forth
behind them a wind, blowing on the long-prowed ship.
And at once they spread the sails on both the sheets,
guiding straight the well-benched ship; and it beneath the rushing
sped over the broad flood; and the dark wave moaned about it,
breaking; and the grey foam seethed all about;
and about it the dolphins thronged in shoals,
swiftly traversing the paths of the grey sea.
And at once they came to the fish-filled Hellespont,
where the other ships were; and the Achaeans rejoiced,
when they saw those they had longed for through the host. And they from the ship
gladly stepped down; and the bold son of Poeas held out
his weak hands upon the men, who both
led him, painfully limping, to the divine land,
leaning upon the strong hands of both;
as when in the thickets an oak cut halfway through
by the force of the woodman, or a rich pine
still standing a little, as much as the woodcutter left,
cutting the rich stem below, that it may become a torch,
pitch subdued by fire among the mountains, and it, grievously
weighed down, the wind and its own weakness leans
upon the flourishing young trees, and they bear it as it presses heavy;
so the man, weighed down with unbearable pain,
the bold heroes bore as he leaned upon them
to the warlike throng of the Argives; and they, beholding,
all greatly pitied the far-shooting man, worn
by his grievous wound; but firm and free of sickness
swifter than swift thought made him
Podaleirius, like the heavenly gods, well
sprinkling many drugs upon the wound, and well calling
upon the name of his father; and swiftly the Achaeans shouted,
all glorifying together the son of Asclepius.
And they cleansed him, and anointed him with oil
eagerly; and the deadly dejection and misery
by the will of the immortals was destroyed; and in their hearts
they took joy as they watched; and he revived from his wretchedness;
and the flush came over his pallor, and over his grievous
weakness great strength; and all his limbs grew strong.
And as when a field grows fat with its ears of corn,
which before, withering, the rain of dread winter
had flooded as it bore down, and it, growing in the winds,
smiles, flourishing in the much-toiled meadow;
so the body of Philoctetes, worn before,
swiftly bloomed again; and in the well-rounded hollow ship
he left behind all the cares that had been wearing his heart.
And the sons of Atreus, seeing the man returning as if from death,
marvelled; for they thought it the work
of the immortals; and so it was in truth, as they perceived;
for greatness and splendour were poured over him
by noble Tritogeneia; and at once he appeared such as he had been
before among the Argives, ere he was subdued by his ills.
And then to the hut of wealthy Agamemnon
all the chiefs together led the son of Poeas;
and glorifying him they honoured him with feasts.
But when they had taken their fill of drink and good food,
then Agamemnon of the good ashen spear spoke to him:
O friend, since by the will of the gods we once
left you in sea-girt Lemnos, harmed in our judgement,
do not now cast dread wrath within your heart;
for not without the blessed ones did we do this, but somehow
the immortals themselves wished to lay many ills upon us
while you were away, since you know how with your arrows
to subdue our foes, when they fight against you.
For the paths of much-wandering life for men
over all the mainland and over the long sea are unseen,
by the will of the Fates, and many-branched,
close-set and crooked, turning this way and that;
and along them the young men are borne by the destiny of fate,
like leaves beneath the blasts of the wind
that drive them; and the good man often falls upon an evil
path, and the bad upon a good one; and these neither to avoid
nor of his own will to choose can any earthly man;
but the prudent man must, even if he is borne by the storms
along a grievous path, with a firm mind endure his misery.
But since we erred and went astray in this deed,
we will appease you again with boundless gifts,
if ever we take the well-built city of the Trojans;
but now take seven women and twenty swift horses,
prize-winners, and twelve tripods, with which your heart
you shall delight all your days; and in my huts
ever beside the feast a royal portion shall be yours.
So speaking, he gave the hero very beautiful gifts.
And the strong-hearted son of Poeas answered him:
O friend, I am no longer angry with you, nor with any other
of the Argives, even if any still erred on my account;
for I know how the mind of good men is changeable,
nor is it right ever to be harsh or arrogant,
but at one time to be fierce, at another to be gentle.
But now let us go to bed, since for a man eager to fight
it is better to sleep than to feast at length.
So speaking, he sprang up and came to the hut
of his comrades; and they quickly for the war-loving king
made ready a bed, greatly rejoicing in their hearts;
and he gladly lay down until the dawn.
And the divine night drew back; and the light reddened the hills
of the sun, and all mortals busied themselves with their works.
And the Argives, greatly longing for the deadly war,
some whetted their well-polished spears, and others their shafts,
and others their javelins; and with the dawn they prepared a meal
for themselves and for the horses; and all partook of food.
