And to them the mighty son of blameless Poeas
spoke this word, urging them on to labour:
Come now, let us take thought for the war; and let none of us
remain by the ships, before we have loosed the famed walls
of well-towered Troy, and burned the city.
So he spoke; and their hearts within their breasts were greatly warmed;
and they put on their armour and shields; and out of the ships
all together, equipped with ashen spears,
they rushed, and with shields of oxhide and double-crested helmets;
and one pressed upon another along the ranks; nor would you say,
as they rushed on, that one was far from another;
so close-thronged they went, fitted to one another.

title: The Fall of Troy
text:
10. The Trojans in their turn were outside the city of Priam,
all with their armour and their chariots and their horses,
swiftest of horses; for they were burning those slain in battle,
fearing lest the host of the Achaeans should bear down upon them.
And when they saw them rushing toward the city,
hastily they cast a heaped barrow about their slain,
hurrying; for terribly they trembled at the sight.
And to them, grieving in their hearts, a word was spoken
by Polydamas, for he was exceedingly prudent and wise of mind:
O friends, no longer is the madness of Ares to be borne against us;
but come, let us take thought, how we may find some device
of war; for the Danaans prevail, standing fast.
But now come, mounting upon the well-built towers,
let us remain, fighting by nights and by days,
until the Danaans come to deep-soiled Sparta,
or here beside the wall grow weary as they wait,
sitting inglorious; for they will not have the strength
to break the long walls, however much they labour;
for the imperishable works fashioned by the gods are not feeble.
Nor are we anywhere in want of food or drink;
for in the halls of Priam rich in gold
there lie firm stores of food, which for many others too
will be food for a long time as they gather,
to their fill, even if a host three times as great
should come here besides, longing to bring aid.
So he spoke; but the bold son of Anchises rebuked him:
Polydamas, how then do they say you are prudent,
you who bid us suffer pains throughout the city for a long time?
For the Achaeans will not grow weary here for long,
but will bear down, seeing us shrinking back;
and ours will be the grief, perishing in our fatherland,
if somehow they besiege us here for a long time;
for no one from Thebe will give us honey-sweet bread,
when we are penned within the city, nor will any bring
wine from Maeonia; but beneath grievous hunger
we shall perish wretchedly, even though the wall defends us well.
But if to escape evil death and the Fates,
and not to die wretchedly in much-burdening hunger,
is our purpose, then in our armour, with our children
and our honoured fathers, let us fight; and somehow Zeus
will help us; for we are of his glorious blood;
but if we come to be hated even by him,
it is better to perish gloriously, defending our fatherland,
than, remaining, to die wretchedly.
So he spoke; and all cried out in assent as they heard.
And at once with helmets and shields and spears
they fenced themselves against one another; and the eyes of tireless Zeus
looked down from Olympus upon them arming for Ares,
Trojans against Argives; and he roused the heart of each,
that he might stretch unceasing battle over both
peoples; for Alexander was now to die
beneath the hands of Philoctetes, fighting for his wife.
And Strife, mistress of tumult, led them to one place,
seen by none; for a cloud encompassed her shoulders,
blood-stained; and she ranged, stirring up great tumult,
now into the gathering of the Trojans, now of the Achaeans;
and Fear and Terror, fearless, waited about her,
glorifying their strong-hearted father's sister;
and she rose up mightily from small, raging;
and she had armour of adamant spattered with gore;
and she brandished a deadly spear into the air; and beneath her feet
the dark earth was stirred; and she breathed forth a blast of fire,
terrible; and ever loudly she shouted, urging on
the young men; and they at once came together, arraying
the battle; for the dread goddess led them to the great work.
And as the cry of the winds blowing furiously,
when spring begins, when the tall trees and the wood
put forth leaves, or as when through a parched thicket fire
blazes and roars, or as when the boundless sea
rages from the harsh-sounding wind, and about it the surf
becomes immeasurable, and the knees of the sailors tremble beneath them;
so the vast earth resounded greatly beneath them as they rushed on;
and strife fell among them; and man rushed upon man.
First Aeneas of the Danaans took Harpalion,
the son of Arizelus, whom his mother Amphinome bore
in the land of the Boeotians, and he with divine Prothoenor
came to Troy to defend the Argives;
him then Aeneas, striking beneath the soft belly,
robbed of his life and of sweet living.
And after him he slew the son of wise Thersander,
Hyllus, striking him with a barbed javelin in the throat,
whom divine Arethusa bore beside the waters of Lethaeus
in sea-girt Crete; and he greatly grieved Idomeneus.
But the son of the son of Peleus slew twelve men
of the Trojans at once beneath his father's spear:
Cebrus first and Harmon and Pasitheus,
and Hysminus and Imbrasius and Schedius and Phleges,
and Mnaseus after them and Ennomus and Amphinous,
and Phasis and Galenus, who had his house
in lofty Gargarum, and was conspicuous among the fighting
strong Trojans, and came with a boundless host
to Troy; for greatly had the son of Dardanus, Priam,
promised to give him many fine and very beautiful gifts,
fool that he was; nor did he mark his own doom; for he was
swiftly to perish in the grievous war,
before he could bear the glorious gifts from the house of Priam.
And then unseen Fate gave over to the Argives
Eurymenes, the comrade of strong-hearted Aeneas.
And she roused great courage beneath his heart, that, slaying
many, he might fulfil his appointed day beneath destruction.
And he laid low one here, one there, like a pitiless beast;
and they did not withstand him in his last hour of life
as he raged terribly and took no thought of doom;
and now he would have done a boundless deed in that battle,
had not his hands grown weary and his spear-point
been wholly bent back; and his sword-hilt no longer
held; but Fate broke it; and beneath his javelin
Meges struck him in the gullet; and the blood gushed up
from his mouth; and at once with pain Fate stood beside him.
And of him being slain, two squires of Epeius,
Deileon and Amphion, were minded to take
his armour; but the bold strength of Aeneas
laid them low as they raged wretchedly about the corpse.
And as when in a vineyard one slays the wasps that dart
about the drying grapes in the season of harvest,
and they breathe out their life before they have tasted the fruit;
so he quickly laid them low before they could plunder the armour.
And the son of Tydeus slew Menon and Amphinous,
both blameless men; and Paris took Demoleon,
the son of Hippasus, who before dwelt in the Laconian land
beside the outpourings of the deep-flowing river Eurotas,
and came to Troy with war-swift Menelaus;
and Paris slew him, hitting him beneath the right
breast with an arrow, and scattered his life from his limbs.
And Teucer took Zechis, the far-famed son of Medon,
who dwelt in sheep-rich Phrygia
beneath the holy cave of the fair-tressed Nymphs,
where once, beholding from on high Endymion sleeping
beside his cattle, divine Selene came down
from heaven; for a keen longing for the youth drove her,
immortal and undefiled though she was, of whose
bed even now a token is fashioned beneath the oaks;
for about her was poured in the thickets the milk of cattle; and men
still gaze in wonder at it; for you would say, looking,
that it is very far off, a grey milk; but it sends forth
white water, and a little way off, whenever it comes,
it congeals about the streams, and the ground turns to stone.
And Meges, the son of Phyleus, rushed upon Alcaeus;
and he pierced him as he gasped beneath the heart
with his spear; and quickly his lovely life was loosed;
nor did his wretched parents receive him coming home
from the much-lamented war, though they longed for it,
fair-girdled Phyllis and Margasus, who dwelt
about the streams of the clear-watered Harpasus, which grievously
joins its loud-roaring stream and boundless swell to the Maeander,
raging all its days about its furious flood.
And the noble comrade of Glaucus, Scylaceus of the good ashen spear,
the son of Oileus wounded near at hand as he came against him,
a little above the shield; and through his broad shoulder he drove
the painful spear-point; and the blood gushed about the oxhide.
But he did not slay him; for the day of doom
received him coming home beside the walls of his dear fatherland;
for when the swift Achaeans had sacked steep Ilium,
then, fleeing from the war, he came to Lycia,
alone, without his comrades; and near the city the women,
gathered for their own children and for their husbands,
asked him; and he told them the doom of all;
and they, standing about him, with stones laid that man
low, and he had no joy of his return to his native land,
but the stones above covered him as he groaned greatly;
and a deadly barrow was raised for him out of the missiles
beside the precinct and the tomb of strong Bellerophon,
in it, near the Titanian rock;
but he, having fulfilled his appointed day beneath destruction,
afterward, by the counsels of glorious Apollo,
is honoured like a god, and his honour never wanes.
And after these the son of Poeas slew Deioneus
and the son of Antenor, Acamas of the good ashen spear;
and of other young men he laid low a great throng;
for he raged among the foe, like tireless Ares
or a roaring river, which tears down long fences
in flood, when, furiously stirred about the rocks,
it comes grievously from the mountains, mingled with rain,
ever-flowing though it is and strong-streaming, nor can
the jutting rocks check it as it boils immeasurably;
so none could endure even to look upon the bold son
of glorious Poeas with their eyes and draw near him;
for in his breast was matchless might.
And he was adorned in the armour of wise Heracles,
cunningly wrought; for about him on his shining belt
were bears grim and shameless; and round about jackals,
terrible, and leopards smiling balefully beneath their brows;
and near them were strong-hearted wolves,
and white-tusked boars and mighty lions,
exceedingly like the living; and on every side
battles were set with grievous slaughter.
So many cunning things were wrought about his belt.
And other things adorned his boundless quiver:
on it was the son of Zeus, storm-footed Hermes,
slaying great Argus beside the streams of Inachus,
Argus, who slept with his eyes by turns;
and on it the strength of Phaethon along the stream of Eridanus,
struck from the chariot; and the earth was ablaze,
and, as if truly, black smoke rose in the air;
and godlike Perseus was cutting down grim Medusa,
where the bathing-places of the stars are and the bounds of earth
and the springs of deep-flowing Ocean, where with the tireless
setting sun the evening night comes together;
and on it was the great son of tireless Iapetus,
hung from the crag of steep Caucasus
in unbreakable bonds; and an eagle tore his liver,
ever growing again; and he seemed to groan.
And these the glorious hands of Hephaestus had wrought
for mighty Heracles; and he gave them to the son
of Poeas to bear, for he was a dear friend who shared his roof.
And he, glorying in his armour, laid low the host.
And at last Paris rushed upon him, wielding grievous arrows
in his hands with his curved bow,
boldly; for that day was his last.
And he loosed a swift shaft from the string; and it whistled
as the arrow sped on; nor did it fly vainly from his hands;
and him indeed it missed, as he swerved a very little,
but it struck Cleodorus, glorious though he was,
a little above the breast, and drove through to his shoulder;
for he had no broad shield, which might have kept off grievous doom;
but he, being unarmed, was drawing back; for from his shoulders
Polydamas had struck away his shield, cutting the strap
with his heavy axe; and he gave way, fighting still
with his painful spear; and the grievous shaft fell upon him,
darting from another side; for so somehow the god willed
to bring dread destruction upon the son of wise Lernus,
whom Amphiale bore in the rich land of the Rhodians.
And when Paris had laid him low with the grievous shaft,
then the mighty son of blameless Poeas,
raging, drawing his swift bow, loudly cried to him:
O dog, how I will give you slaughter and unseen doom,
since now you long to match yourself against me;
and they will have respite, all who for your sake grievously
suffer in war; for soon there will be release from destruction
when you are slain here, since you are made their bane.
So speaking, he drew the well-twisted string near to his breast,
and the horn was bent into a circle, and the relentless shaft
was aimed, and the dread point projected
a little beyond the bow by the young man's force; and loudly rang the string
as the harsh-sounding arrow sped on; nor did the divine man
miss; yet his heart was not loosed, but still in his spirit
he had strength; for not mortally did the shaft then fall upon him,
but grazed his hand, scoring his fair flesh.
And again he made ready his bow; but, anticipating him,
the dear son of Poeas struck him with a barbed shaft
above the groin; and he no longer stayed to fight,
but swiftly sprang away, like a dog which, dreading
a lion, draws back though rushing on before;
so he, pierced to the heart with grievous pains,
withdrew from the war. And the hosts joined in tumult,
slaying one another; and the strife was in blood
of the slain on either side; and corpses lay upon corpses,
all together, like drops of rain or hail
or flakes of snow, when the long mountains and the wood
by the counsels of Zeus the West Wind and the storm besprinkle;
so they on both sides, subdued by pitiless Doom,
fell in heaps upon one another, struck down.
And terribly Paris groaned; and about his wound his spirit
was worn; and the physicians swiftly tended him in his distress.
And the Trojans went to their own city; and the Danaans to the dark
ships came swiftly; for them the black night
stayed from tumult, and took the toil from their limbs,
pouring sleep upon their eyelids, a defender against labour.
But sleep did not seize swift Paris until the dawn;
for none could ward off his hurt, though they longed to help
with all manner of remedies, since it was fated for him
to escape death and the Fates beneath the hands of Oenone,
if she should be willing; and he at once, trusting in the prophecies,
went, though unwilling; and deadly necessity led him
to the face of his wedded wife; and grievous birds, meeting him,
cried above his head, and others rushed across
his left hand; and he at one moment
feared as he beheld them, but at another hoped they flew
without fulfilment; but they, amid his pains, revealed dread destruction.
And he came to glorious Oenone; and beholding him,
her handmaids were amazed, all together, and divine Oenone
herself; and he at once fell at the woman's feet,
subdued by the grievous wound, which grew
black about him above and within, until it reached
the rich marrow through the bone, since the dread venom
had rotted his belly along the wounded flesh of the man.
And he was worn, stricken to the heart with hateful pain;
and as when one, burning with sickness and grievous great thirst,
his heart aflame, his close-pressed soul is parched,
whom the boiling bile inflames, and about him his sluggish
soul flutters on his parched lips,
longing both for life and for water;
so beneath his breast his spirit was consumed with pain;
and faintly he spoke this word:
O reverend wife, do not now, worn though I am,
hate me, since once I left you in the halls
a widow, though against my will; for the inescapable Fates led me
to Helen, with whom would that, before I lay
in your arms, I had died and lost my life.
But come, by the gods who dwell about the heaven,
and by your marriage-bed and our wedded love,
set a gentle heart, and ward off grievous anguish,
laying healing drugs upon my deadly wound,
which are fated to thrust the pains from my spirit,
if you are willing; for it is in your mind whether to save me
from harsh-sounding death, or not;
but pity me quickly, and the strength of the swift-fated shafts
cure, while still the might and limbs about me flourish;
nor, remembering grievous jealousy, in any case
leave me to die beneath relentless doom,
fallen at your feet; for you will offend the Prayers,
who themselves are the daughters of loud-thundering Zeus,
and, wroth with overweening men,
afterward send upon them the grievous Erinys
and wrath; but you, lady, ward off the evil Fates
quickly, even if I sinned somewhat in my folly.
So he spoke; but he in no way persuaded her dark mind,
but mocking him she answered, greatly grieved as he was:
Why have you come to me, against whom before
you left in the halls, wailing unspeakably,
for the sake of the much-grieving daughter of Tyndareus, beside whom lying
you took your joy, exulting, since she is far better
than your wedded wife; for she, men say, is ageless;
go to her quickly and supplicate her, nor to me
in tears speak piteous and grievous words;
would that I had in my heart the great might of a beast,
to tear your flesh, and then to gulp your blood,
for such pains as you have wrought me, trusting in your wickedness.
Wretch, where now is your fair-crowned Cytherea?
Where is tireless Zeus, forgetful of his son-in-law?
Have them as your helpers; but from my halls far off
withdraw, you bane grievous to gods and men alike;
for on your account, sinner, grief seized even the immortals,
some for their grandsons, some for their sons being slain.
But begone from my house, and go to Helen,
beside whom it is your lot, by night and by day distressed,
to moan beside her bed, pierced with grievous pain,
until she heal you of your painful agonies.
So speaking, she sent him weeping from her dear halls,
foolish; nor did she mark her own doom; for she too
was, when he had perished, to follow him to the Fates
swiftly; for so the destiny of Zeus had spun for her.
And him, hastening away over the heights of shaggy Ida
along the path to the farthest part, where dread doom led him
grievously limping and greatly grieved at heart,
Hera marked, and her immortal heart was warmed,
seated on Olympus, where the orchard of Zeus is.
And four handmaids sat near her,
whom once bright-eyed Selene, subdued by the Sun,
bore in the wide heaven, tireless, in no way like
to one another; for in form they differed each from each:
the first received the portion of toilsome summer,
the second took thought for winter and the Goat-star;
the third for spring, and the fourth delighted in harvest;
for in four portions the life of mortals is changed,
which those handmaids tend by turns; but these matters
let them be a care to Zeus himself in heaven; and they were talking
of all that deadly Fate in her destroying mind
was devising, contriving the hateful marriage of the daughter of Tyndareus
to Deiphobus, and the grievous wrath of Helenus
and his anger about the woman, and how the sons of the Achaeans
were to snatch him in the high mountains,
wroth with the Trojans, and lead him to the swift ships,
and how by his counsels the son of strong Tydeus,
with Odysseus following, leaping over the great wall,
was to bring grievous destruction upon Alcathous,
seizing willing kindly Tritogeneia,
who was the safeguard of the city and of the Trojans themselves;
for not even any of the gods, however boundlessly wroth,
had the strength to lay waste the prosperous city of Priam
while the immortal, untroubled, stood before it;
nor had men fashioned her immortal image of iron,
but the son of Cronos himself from Olympus
cast it down into the city of Priam rich in gold.
So the wife of Zeus talked with her handmaids,
and of many other things besides. And Paris his spirit on Ida
left behind, nor did Helen behold him returned;
and about him the Nymphs greatly wailed, because they
still remembered in their minds all that before,
from his childhood, when they came together, he had talked with them;
and with them mourned the swift herdsmen of the cattle,
grieving in their hearts; and the glens groaned in answer.
And then to the wife of much-enduring Priam
the herdsman told the dread doom of Alexander;
and at once, when she heard, her spirit shook with trembling,
and her limbs gave way beneath her; and she lamented this word:
You are dead to me, dear child, and grief upon grief
you have left me ever inescapable, since by far the best of my other
children you were after Hector; therefore in misery I shall
weep for you, while the heart yet throbs within my breast;
for not without the blessed ones do we suffer this, but some Fate
devised deadly works, which I ought not to have endured,
but should have died before in peace and prosperity;
but now upon woe I behold woe ever with my eyes,
expecting to look on yet other things more evil,
my children slain, and the city laid waste
and burned with fire by the strong-hearted Danaans,
and my sons' wives and my daughters with the other Trojan women
dragged along with their children under the spear's compulsion.
So she spoke, wailing; but her husband had heard nothing of it,
but sat beside the tomb of Hector, shedding tears,
because he was the best and guarded his fatherland with his spear;
of him grieving in his keen heart he had heard nothing.
But Helen, lamenting very much without ceasing,
some things cried aloud among the Trojans, but other things her heart
within her breast pondered; and to her own spirit she spoke:
Husband, to me and to the Trojans and to you yourself a great woe,
you have perished wretchedly; and me in hateful misery
you have left, expecting to behold more deadly woes.
Would that the Harpies had snatched me away before,
when I followed you by the deadly destiny of fate;
but now the gods have given woe to you and to myself,
ill-fated; and all shudder at me unspeakably,
and all hate my heart; nor do I know in any way
how to escape; for if I flee to the host of the Danaans,
at once they will dishonour my body; but if I remain,
the Trojan men and women, standing about me, one from this side, one from that,
will quickly tear me to pieces; and the earth will not cover my corpse,
but dogs will rend it and the swift tribes of birds;
would that Fate had taken me before I beheld these woes.
So she spoke, mourning not so much for her husband as for
herself, remembering her sin; and round about the Trojan women
groaned as for him, but in their hearts pondered other things,
some remembering their parents, some their husbands,
some their children, and some their honoured kindred.
But Oenone alone was torn in her glorious heart;
yet not among the Trojan women being present
did she wail, but apart, within her own halls,
she lay groaning heavily upon the bed of her old husband.
And as in the thickets the ice is congealed
of the highest mountains, which besprinkles many glens,
poured down by the gusts of the West Wind; but beneath the East Wind
and the sun the snow melts, and the long
crags, streaming with watery rills,
grow wet, and it in the glens, boundless though it is,
melts about the rushing spring, a chill water;
so she, greatly distressed beneath hateful pain,
melted, grieving for her wedded husband.
And terribly groaning she addressed her dear spirit:
Ah me for my folly, ah me for my hateful life,
I who loved my ill-fated husband, with whom I hoped,
worn by old age, to reach the glorious threshold of life,
ever of one mind; but the gods cast it otherwise;
would that the black Fates had snatched me away,
when I was about to be apart from Alexander;
but even if he left me while alive, I will dare a great deed,
to die for his sake, since the dawn no longer pleases me.
So she spoke; and piteously down her eyelids were poured
tears, as, remembering that her wedded husband had fulfilled
destruction, like wax beneath fire, she melted secretly,
for she revered her own father and her fair-robed handmaids,
until over the divine earth from the wide Ocean
night was poured, bringing to mortals release from toil.
And then, while her father slept within the halls
and the slaves, she burst open the gates of the chambers
and rushed forth, like a storm-blast; and her swift limbs bore her;
and as when in the mountains a heifer that has greatly desired the bull
is urged by her spirit to be borne on quick feet,
hastening, and she, longing for love,
fears not the herdsman, but an irresistible impulse bears her,
if somewhere in the thickets she might see the familiar bull;
so she, running swiftly, traversed the long ways,
seeking quickly to mount the dread pyre with her feet.
Nor did her knees grow weary; lighter were borne
her feet ever as she hastened; for deadly Doom drove her on
and Cypris; nor did she dread the shaggy beasts
that met her under the night, before greatly shuddering;
and all the rock of the shaggy mountains was trodden by her
and the crags, and all the ravines were crossed.
And her, looking down from on high, divine Selene
remembered in her heart blameless Endymion,
and greatly pitied her as she hastened; and above her
shining brightly she lit up the long ways.
And she came, borne on through the mountain, where the other
Nymphs were wailing about the pyre of Alexander.
And him a strong fire still encompassed, because for him
the shepherds, gathering from the mountain, one from this side, one from that,
had heaped up a wondrous pile of wood, bringing favour
at the last, and grief alike to their comrade and their lord,
weeping very much, standing about; but she in no way,
when she beheld it openly, wailed, worn though she was,
but, veiling her fair face in her robe,
at once leapt upon the pyre; and she stirred up much lamentation;
and she burned about her husband; and the Nymphs, one from this side, one from that,
were amazed, when they beheld her fallen beside the man;
and one in her own heart spoke this word:
Truly Paris was reckless, who left his most faithful
wedded wife, and brought home a wanton consort,
a deadly grief to himself and the Trojans and the city,
fool that he was; nor did he revere the heart of his wise wife,
worn though she was, who beyond the light of the sun
honoured him, even as he hated her and loved her not.
So spoke one of the Nymphs in her heart; and they in the midst
of the pyre burned, forgetful of the Dawn-goddess;
and about them the herdsmen marvelled, as before
the Argives marvelled, all together, when they beheld
Evadne flung upon the limbs of Capaneus,
about her husband, subdued by the grievous thunderbolt of Zeus.
But when the deadly rush of fire had made an end of both,
Oenone and Paris, and laid them low in a single ash,
then they quenched the pyre with wine; and their bones
they placed in a golden bowl; and about them a barrow
they swiftly raised; and they set two pillars above,
which face turned each one away from the other,
still bearing toward each other a grievous jealousy.

title: The Fall of Troy
text:
11. But the women of Troy were mourning throughout the city, nor were they able
to come out to the tomb, for it lay very far away
from the steep town; and the young men outside the walls
toiled without rest, and the slaughtering battle did not cease,
though Alexander had fallen with a crash, because the Achaeans
pressed on against the Trojans toward the city, and these men too
went out beyond the wall, since necessity led them on;
for in their midst Strife and groaning Enyo
ranged to and fro, like the grim Furies to look upon,
both breathing deadly destruction from their mouths;
and around them the Fates, with shameless heart,
raged cruelly; and on the other side Panic and Ares
spurred the hosts on; and Terror followed beside them,
spattered with bloody gore, that men might,
some be strengthened at the sight, while others fled;
and everywhere the javelins and spears and shafts of men,
this way and that, poured forth, eager for evil slaughter;
and around them a din arose as they pressed close,
fighting on both sides in the man-destroying joy of war.
There Neoptolemus slew Laodamas,
who was reared in Lycia beside the fair streams of Xanthus,
whom once the wife of loud-thundering Zeus,
divine Leto, brought forth for men, when she had broken with her hands
the rough soil of glorious Lycia, in the hour when by the toil
of her divine travail, with much-enduring anguish,
she was overcome by birth-pangs, such as the pangs awakened.
After him he destroyed Nirus, striking him in the fight
with his spear through the jaw; the bronze pierced his mouth
and his speaking tongue; he, around the unbearable point of the spear,
gripped it, bellowing; and the blood ran about his jaws
as he tried to speak; and by the might of that strong hand
the groaning spear drove him down to the floor of the earth,
emptied of life. He struck noble Euenor
a little above the flank, and drove the point
clean into the middle of his liver; and grievous death met him at once.
He took Iphition, and laid low Hippomedon,
the mighty son of Maenalus, whom the Nymph Ocyrrhoe bore
beside the stream of the river Sangarius; nor did she
welcome his return; an evil Fate robbed her cruelly
of her son, and cast great grief upon the father.
And Aeneas slew Bremon and Andromachus,
the one reared in Cnossus, the other in holy Lyctus;
and both from their swift-footed horses fell to one spot;
and the one gasped, pierced through the throat
by the long spear, while the other, struck on the base of the painful temple
by a groaning stone hurled from a very strong hand,
breathed out his life, and black doom enfolded him.
The horses, panicked and far from their charioteers,
fleeing, wandered among the many corpses;
and the squires of blameless Aeneas
seized them and rejoiced in heart over the dear spoil.
There Philoctetes struck Peirasus with a deadly arrow
as he fled from the war; it severed the bent sinews
behind the knee, and broke the man's onrush;
and when one of the Danaans saw him crippled,
he swiftly stripped him of his head, striking with the sword
the grievous tendon; and the earth received his maimed
body; and his head, rolling apart, was carried off
while his voice still struggled forth; and swiftly his life flew away.
And Polydamas struck Cleon and Eurymachus with the spear,
who came from Syme under lord Nireus,
both skilled in devising guile against the fish
with the dread hook, and to cast into the bright sea
their nets, and cunningly with their hands from the ship
to wield the trident straight and swift against the fish;
but their works of the sea did not ward off ruin from them then.

title: The Fall of Troy
text:
And Eurypylus, steadfast in war, slew glorious Hellus,
whom his mother bore beside the Gygaean lake,
fair-cheeked Cleito; and he was stretched in the dust
face down; and far from him fell likewise the long spear
from his sturdy shoulder, the hand still cut off by the cruel sword,
still quivering to raise the spear toward the fray,
all in vain; for no man guided it to the work,
but it twitched of itself, as the tail of a grim serpent,
cut off, leaps up, yet no strength
follows it to the steep struggle, to chase the one who has wounded it;
so the right hand of that strong-hearted man
strove to labour at the spear-point; but its force no longer followed.
But Odysseus killed Aenus and Polyidus,
both of the Ceteians, the one with the spear, the other with the grievous
sword laying him low. And Sthenelus took noble Abas,
hurling his javelin; and it, straight through the windpipe
speeding, reached the grievous tendon of the neck;
it loosed the man's heart, and unstrung all his limbs.
And the son of Tydeus took Laodocus, and Agamemnon Melius,
and Deiphobus took Dryas and Alcimus; and Agenor
slew Hippasus, glorious though he was,
who came from the river Peneius; nor did he repay
the lovely nurture to his parents, since a god broke him.
There Thoas laid low Lalus and brave Lyncus,
and Meriones killed Lycon, and Menelaus Archilochus,
who dwelt below the Corycian ridge
and the rock of wise Hephaestus, which is to mortals
a wonder; for upon it burns an unwearied fire,
unquenchable, by night and by day; and around it
the date-palms flourish, and bear boundless fruit,
their roots burning together with the stones; but that work, I think,
the immortals fashioned, a marvel even for men to come.
And Teucer eagerly aimed to strike with his shaft
Menoetes, the son of blameless Hippomedon, as he came on;
and with mind and hands and eyes he guided
the arrow from the curved horn; and it, grievous,
leaped from his swift hand at the man; and beneath it the string
still twanged; and the other gasped in answer,
struck, since the Fates were borne together with the shaft
straight to the heart, where the mind of men is seated
and the spirit, and swift are the paths to death.
And Euryalus from his sturdy hand hurled a great stone
far off, and made the swift ranks of the Trojans reel;
as when a man, angered at long-voiced cranes,
a guardian of the field, greatly vexed, rushes upon them,
whirling about his head with quick hand the ox-sinew sling,
and casts the stone against them, and with the whir scatters
the long lines spread through the air, and they take flight,
darting one upon another, wheeling about,
with much clamour, who before had gone in good order;
so the foe were scattered by the fearful missile
of mighty Euryalus; and the god did not bear it in vain,
but, helmet and all, the head of strong Meles
it crushed about the eye-sockets; and the doom appointed found him.
So one slew another, and the land groaned around;
as when, an immense wind bearing down
fierce, beneath the gust of its deep-roaring blast, this way and that,
tall trees fall, torn up from their roots,
in a broad-floored grove, and all the earth roars around;
so they fell in the dust, and their armour rang
unspeakably, and the earth crashed loud around them; and they took thought
of the grim turmoil, dealing ruin among themselves.
And then near Aeneas came kindly Apollo
and the son of Antenor, warlike Eurymachus;
for they were fighting against the mighty Achaeans,
standing very close in the battle, as beneath a wagon
two yoke-mates, strong oxen of like age, do not flag
from their labour; and the god straightway spoke a word to them,
likening himself to the seer Polymestor, whom once his mother
bore beside the streams of Xanthus, a servant of the Far-shooter:
"Eurymachus, and Aeneas, race of the gods, it is in no way fitting
that you should yield to the Argives; for not even Ares himself,
mighty though he is, will rejoice to meet you,
if you are willing to fight in the fray, since the Fates
have spun a long end of life for you both."
So speaking, he mingled with the winds and became unseen;
and they perceived in their minds the god's might; for at once upon them
boundless courage was poured; and the spirit raged
within their breasts, and they leaped upon the Argives,
like cruel wasps, which in bitter
anger from their heart bear down upon bees,
which they see coming about the grapes drying
in the harvest season, or darting from the hive;
so the sons of Troy upon the war-loving Achaeans
leaped eagerly; and the dark Fates rejoiced
at the fighting; and Ares laughed; and Enyo shrieked
terribly; and loud about them rang the gleaming armour.

title: The Fall of Troy
text:
And they kept slaughtering the countless tribes of the foe
with unwearied hands; and the hosts kept falling
likewise, as the swath in the season of warm summer,
which the swift reapers hasten on with their hands,
having shared out across the field the long measures of land;
so beneath their hands the ranks kept falling,
in thousands; and the earth, filled all around with the dead,
flowed with blood; and Strife was warmed in heart
at the dying; but they did not cease at all from the evil struggle,
but came on like lions upon sheep; and the others took thought
of wretched flight, and out of the deadly war
fled, all whose strength still lay unbroken in their feet.
And the son of wise Anchises followed ever
behind the foe, cutting their backs with his spear,
and Eurymachus on the other side; and the immortal heart
of far-shooting Apollo was warmed, looking down from above.
As when a man against the swine that come
into the dry cornfield, before the swath is laid low by the reapers,
sets on his strong dogs to face them, and they, seeing them
rush, tremble, and care no longer
for the food, but turn to grievous flight
all in a rush, and the dogs, swiftly overtaking them by foot,
tear them mercilessly from behind, while they flee
howling far off, and the lord of the field rejoices;
so Phoebus was warmed, when he saw out of the war
the great host of the Argives fleeing; for no longer
were the deeds of men a care to them; but they prayed to the gods
to bear their feet swiftly; for in their feet alone now lay
the hope of return; for upon all of them came, raging with the spear,
Eurymachus and Aeneas, and their comrades with them.
There a certain one of the Argives, either trusting wholly in strength,
or by the will of Fate, who longed to destroy him,
checked his horse as it fled from the ill-sounding war,
eager to turn it back to the fray, that he might fight
against the foe; but bold-hearted Agenor,
forestalling him, cut his painful arm
with the two-edged axe; and to the iron's force gave way
the bone of the wounded arm; and the sinews
it cut away easily; and the veins gushed forth blood;
and he was flung down along the horse's neck; and at once he himself
fell among the corpses; but he left his strong hand,
still firmly clinging to the well-bent rein,
just as it had been while he lived; and it was a great wonder,
for from the rein there hung the bloody hand,
by the prompting of Ares, bearing terror to the foe;
you would have said it still longed to labour at the riding.
And the horse bore it, a token of its slain master.
And Aeneas slew, striking with the spear above the loin,
Aethalides; and the point passed out beside the navel,
dragging the entrails with it; and he was stretched in the dust,
clutching with his hands at once the point and his bowels,
groaning terribly, and he set his teeth into the earth,
bellowing; and his soul and his pains left the man.
And the Argives, like oxen, were panicked,
which, straining eagerly beneath the yoke and the plough,
the gadfly strikes under the flank with its long lips,
thirsting for blood, and they, vexed beyond measure,
flee far from the work, and the man grieves over them,
both labouring at his labour and trembling for his oxen,
lest somehow behind them, as the plough drives on,
the merciless iron, striking against their feet, cut their sinews;
so the Danaans fled; and around them grieved in heart
the son of Achilles; and loudly he cried, restraining the host:
"Ah, cowards, why do you flee, like worthless
starlings, which a hawk, coming against them, has frightened?
But come, set courage in your hearts, since it is far better
to die in war than to choose unmanly flight."
So he spoke; and they obeyed, setting a bold mind in their breasts
quickly; and he, with high heart, rushed upon the Trojans,
brandishing in his hands the swift spear; and the hosts
of the Myrmidons followed him, with might like a storm
in their breasts; and the Argives drew breath
from the turmoil; and he, swiftly like his own dear father in spirit,
slew one after another in the fray; and they, withdrawing,
gave way, like waves, which from the north wind's storm
roll thick and seething upon the shores,
rising from the sea, and them another blast from elsewhere,
darting against them, raging in a great whirlwind,
drives back from the beaches, while the North still blows a little;
so the Trojans, who before pressed on against the Danaans,
the son of godlike Achilles thrust back
a little, since the noble might of bold-hearted Aeneas
would not let them flee, but bade them stand in the dread fray
boldly; and on either side Enyo stretched the strife
even. But not at all against Aeneas
did the son of Achilles hurl the spear of his own father,
but turned his heart elsewhere, since Thetis of the splendid robe,
in reverence for Cytherea, turned her grandson's
spirit and great strength against other tribes of the host.

title: The Fall of Troy
text:
There the one slew many of the Trojans, while the other of the Achaeans
laid low countless tribes; and over the slain in the strife
the birds rejoiced, eager to tear the entrails of men
and their flesh; and the Nymphs lamented,
the daughters of fair-flowing Simoeis and of Xanthus.
And so they laboured; and the unwearied winds raised
boundless dust; and a divine mist clouded over
all the air above, like an unseen fog,
nor was the earth seen, and it blinded the eyes of mortals;
but even so they fought; and whomever they took in their hands
they slew without mercy, even if he were most dear;
for it was not possible in the turmoil to mark the foe
coming on, nor yet a comrade; and helplessness held the hosts.
And now they would have been confounded together and perished cruelly,
all alike, falling upon one another's deadly
swords, had not the son of Cronos from Olympus
warded it from them in their distress, and driven the dust apart
from the fight, and calmed the deadly blasts.
But they still strove on; yet their toil was made
far lighter; for they could see whether they must slay
the foeman in the turmoil, or whether to avoid him.
And now the Danaans drove back the throng of the Trojans,
and now again the Trojans the ranks of the Danaans; and dread
was the battle; and like snowflakes the missiles fell,
coming from both sides; and fear held the shepherds
watching the war from far off, from the Idaean mountains.
And one, lifting his hands to the heavenly ones in the sky,
prayed that all the foe might perish beneath Ares,
but that the Trojans might draw breath from the groaning war,
and one day look upon a free day; but to him in no way
did they hearken; for Fate, full of groans, was pondering otherwise;
and she revered neither huge Zeus, nor any other
of the immortals; for the grim mind of her
is never turned, whatever doom upon men at their birth,
upon men or upon cities, she spins with her
inescapable thread; and beneath her all things, some waste away, some grow;
and by her promptings the toil and the strife arose
for the horse-fighting Trojans and the spear-fighting Achaeans.
And they wrought slaughter and pitiless doom for one another
without rest; for no fear held them, but they fought
with eager will; for courage draws men on to the spear.
But when many had perished in the dust,
then for the Argives the higher strength was roused
by the promptings of warlike Pallas, who, coming
very near to the battle, greatly defended the Argives,
eager to sack the famous city of Priam.
And then noble Aphrodite snatched glorious Aeneas,
she who greatly groaned at the slaying of Alexander,
herself away from the war and the deadly fray,
swiftly; and about him she poured much mist;
for it was no longer fated that that man in the strife
should fight the Argives before the steep wall.
Therefore she shunned the wise Tritogeneia exceedingly,
from her heart, as she was eager to help the Danaans,
lest even beyond his doom the goddess should take him; for not even
of Ares himself had she spared before, who was far stronger.
And the Trojans no longer held their place at the mouth of battle,
but drew back, with astonished heart;
for upon them, like raw-devouring beasts,
the Argives leaped, raging greatly for Ares.
And as these were laid low, the rivers were filled with corpses
and the plain; for many fell in heaps in the dust,
men and horses; and very many chariots lay scattered
of the fallen; and everywhere boundless blood flowed
like rain; for deadly Fate came on the turmoil.
And some, pierced by swords or by ashen spears,
lay beside one another, like spilled
timbers, when upon the shore of the heavy-thundering sea
men loose the countless lashings from the toil-wrought bolts
and scatter the long beams and the wood
of a lofty raft, and everywhere the broad beach
is filled, and the black swell washes against them;
so these, in the dust and blood laid low,
lay, forgetful of the much-bewailed onset.
And a few, escaping the pitiless fray,
plunged into the city, avoiding heavy woe;
and their wives and children received from their bloodied bodies
all the armour, foul with grim gore.
And for all warm baths were prepared; and through all the town
the healers hastened to the houses of the wounded warriors,
busying themselves, that they might heal the wounded.
And their wives and children lamented around them as they came
from the war; and many, not present, they called by name;
and some, smitten in heart with hateful grief,
lay groaning heavily over their pains; while others to supper
turned from their toil; and the swift horses neighed beside them,
whinnying eagerly at their fodder; and on the other side the Achaeans
beside their huts and ships laboured even as the Trojans.

title: The Fall of Troy
text:
And when Dawn had driven her gleaming horses
over the streams of Ocean, and the tribes of men awoke,
then the warlike sons of the mighty Argives,
some went toward the steep city of Priam,
while others in the huts beside the wounded men
remained, lest at any time the grievous host, bearing down,
should take the ships, bringing favour to the Trojans; and these from the towers
fought against the Argives; and grievous turmoil arose.
Before the Scaean gate the son of Capaneus
fought together with godlike Diomedes; and these from above
Deiphobus, steadfast in war, and strong Polites,
together with other comrades, kept back with arrows
and with stones; and there clashed around the men,
struck, the helmets and the shields, which warded
the grievous doom of the warriors and their pitiless fate.
And about the Idaean gates the son of Achilles
contended; and around him all the Myrmidons
laboured, skilled in the strong onset;
and from the wall there held them off with countless shafts
boldly Helenus and bold-hearted Agenor,
urging on the Trojans in the fray; and they too of themselves
fought eagerly about the walls of their dear fatherland.
And toward the plain by the gates, and toward the swift-faring ships
as they went, Odysseus and Eurypylus laboured
without rest; and these from the high rampart
noble Aeneas, with high thoughts, kept off with stones.
And toward the stream of Simoeis a painful toil held
Teucer of the good ashen spear; and elsewhere each had his own woe.
And then around wise Odysseus the glorious men,
by his cunning device, toward the labour of Ares
fitted their shields, and cast them above their heads,
setting them upon one another; and the whole joined in one joining;
you would have said it was the close-roofed covering of a hall,
which neither the rush of the wind, blowing wet,
boundless, passes through, nor the unspeakable rain from Zeus;
such were the ranks of the Argives, covered round
with ox-hides, made firm; and they held one mind for valour,
joined into one; and from above the sons of Troy
hurled stones; and these, as from a hard rock,
rolled down upon the firm earth; and many spears
and groaning missiles and grievous javelins
stuck in the shields, and some in the ground, and many far off
were borne in vain, bent aside by the shafts,
as they were struck from every side; and they did not flee the din
at all, immense as it was, nor gave way, as those who hear
the patter of raindrops; and upward beneath the wall they went together; nor did any of them
stand apart; but, joined together, they pressed on,
like a misty cloud, which, in the depth of winter,
the son of Cronos stretches long from the highest sky.
And much roar was about the phalanx, and a clatter beneath the feet
of those advancing arose; and the winds far off
bore the rising dust a very little above the ground
behind the warriors; and a confused cry rang round,
as beneath the hives the bees hum;
and panting rose abundant in a flood, and the breath spread around
of the host as it gasped; and boundlessly in heart
the sons of Atreus rejoiced, exulting over themselves,
beholding the fearless fence against the ill-sounding war;
and they purposed at the gates of god-born Priam,
crowded close, with two-edged axes,
to break the long walls, and to thrust the gates down to the ground,
having dragged them from their hinges; and noble counsel held
hope; but neither the ox-hides availed them
nor the swift axes, since the might of Aeneas,
mighty, sent against them a stone fitted to both his hands,
in his eagerness, and he laid low with grievous doom
the men whom he caught beneath their shields, as in the mountains
the goats feeding beneath a crag by the force
of a broken cliff, and all that graze nearby tremble;
so the Danaans were amazed; and he still, from above,
hurled stones thick and fast, and the ranks were utterly thrown into confusion;
as when in the mountains the Olympian Zeus from heaven
breaks the crags joined about a single peak, this way and that,
beneath his thunders and the smoking thunderbolt,
and around the sheep tremble and flee this way and that;
so the sons of the Achaeans shrank back, because among them
Aeneas swiftly shattered the bulwark of the war,
made of unwearied shields, because to him
a god had thrust boundless strength; nor could any of them
endure to look him in the face in the strife,
because around his sturdy limbs there gleamed
his armour, like to the divine lightnings;
and near him stood, his form hidden in darkness,
dread Ares, and he guided all the missiles
that bore either death or dread fear upon the Argives;
and he fought as when the Olympian Zeus himself in heaven,
in his wrath, laid low the overweening tribes of the Giants,
terrible, and shook the boundless earth
and Tethys and Ocean and the sky, and all around
the limbs of Atlas quaked beneath the unwearied rush of Zeus;
so beneath Aeneas the ranks of the Argives
fell in ruin in the strife; for he, around the wall on every side,
rushed against the foe in his wrath, and from his hands
everything that met his eagerness as he hastened to the toil
he hurled, since very many defences against the evil of war
lay upon the walls of the war-steadfast Dardanians,
with which Aeneas, raging in his great strength,
kept off the great host of the foe; and around him
the Trojans held firm; and evil misery held them all
about the city; and many fell, both of the Achaeans
and also of the Trojans; and loud they cried on both sides,
Aeneas bidding the war-loving Trojans
fight for their city, their wives, and themselves
eagerly; while the son of war-steadfast Achilles
bade the Argives beside the famous walls of Troy
remain, until, having burned the city with fire, they took it.
And both groaning and unspeakable was the cry that wrapped
them as they fought all day in the turmoil; nor was there any
breathing-space from the war for them, longing in heart,
the one side to take the city beneath Ares, the other to save it.

title: The Fall of Troy
text:
And Ajax, apart from bold-hearted Aeneas,
fighting against the Trojans, sent evil dooms upon them
with his far-shooting bow, since for him now
the straight shaft flew through the air, and now again
the grievous javelins; and one upon another he slew;
and they, cowering before the valour of the blameless man,
no longer held their place in the fray; and the host left the walls.
And then his squire, by far the best in battle of the Locrians,
Alcimedon the high-hearted, trusting in his king
and in his own strength and bold youth,
eager for war, set his swift feet upon
the ladder, that he might make a path to the city for his men,
a grievous one; and, to be a defence for his own head,
having set his shield above it, he went up the cruel ways,
setting a fearless mind in his heart; and in his hand
now he brandished the merciless spear, and now again
he crept upward; and the airy path bore him swiftly.
And now there would have been grief for the Trojans, had not, as he
already peered over and looked upon the city,
for the last time and the first, from the high rampart,
Aeneas rushed upon him, since the assault did not escape him,
nor was he far off; and he struck him with a broad stone
on the head; and the great force of the strong-hearted man
shattered the ladder beneath him; and he from on high, like an arrow
sped from the bowstring, fell; and deadly doom followed him
as he whirled about; and his groaning spirit with the air
was swiftly mingled, before he reached the hard ground;
and he crashed down upon the earth in his breastplate, because
his sturdy spear and broad shield were flung away from him,
and his strong helmet; and the host of the Locrians
groaned around, when they saw the man laid low by evil ruin;
for from his shaggy head this way and that
his brain was bespattered; and all were crushed together,
his bones and swift limbs, befouled with grim gore.
And then the noble son of godlike Poeas,
when he saw Aeneas raging about the walls,
in might like a wild beast, straightway sent forth an arrow,
aiming it at the glorious man; nor did he miss
the man, yet in no way through the unwearied shield
did it reach his fair flesh, for Cytherea turned it aside
and the shield, but it just grazed the ox-hide skin.
Yet it did not fall to the ground in vain, but Medon,
between the shield and the horse-haired helmet,
it struck; and he fell down from the tower, as from a rock
a man strikes a wild goat with a groaning shaft;
so he fell and was stretched out; and the sacred life left him.
And Aeneas, in anger for his comrade, hurled a stone,
and slew the noble comrade of Philoctetes,
Toxaechmes; and he crushed his head, and shattered all
his bones with the helmet; and his bright heart was loosed.
And at him the son of noble Poeas cried aloud:
"Aeneas, now you hope in your heart to be the best,
labouring from the tower, where women
fight against the foe, all unwarlike; but if you are anyone,
come outside the wall in your armour, that you may learn
to know the bold son of Poeas both by spear and by arrows."
So he spoke; but to him the bold son of Anchises,
though he wished it, made no answer, because there arose
a wretched struggle about the long walls and the town
without rest; for they ceased not at all from the evil fray;
nor for them, sorely tried beneath Ares for a long while,
was there any release from toil; and the labour rose unending.
12. But when the spear-bearing Danaans had toiled much about the walls of Troy,
and there was no end of the war in sight,
then Calchas made a gathering of the chiefs,
knowing well in his heart, by the promptings of the Far-shooter,
the flights of birds and the stars and all the other
signs that come to men by the will of the gods,
and to them as they assembled he spoke a word like this:
"No longer sit before the walls and toil,
but devise some other plan in your minds
and a stratagem, which shall be a help to the host and to us;
for indeed yesterday I saw here a sign:
a hawk pursued a dove; and she, hard pressed,
sank into a cleft of the rock; and he, enraged at her,
remained near for a very long while in his grief
beside the cleft; but she shunned him; and he, setting dire wrath in his heart,
hid himself in a bush; and she darted out in her folly,
thinking him far off; but he, leaping up,
loosed groaning death upon the wretched dove;
so let us now not by force seek to sack
the Trojan town, but see if some guile and craft will avail."
So he spoke; but none of them said he could devise in mind
a defence against the wretched fray; and they sought to find
a remedy; and alone in his wisdom did the son
of Laertes perceive it, and spoke a word in answer:
"O friend, wholly honoured by the heavenly gods,
if it is truly fated for the warlike Achaeans
to sack the city of Priam by guile,
let us build a horse, and we chiefs, the best men,
will go gladly into the ambush; and the host shall depart
to Tenedos with the ships, and let all
burn their huts, that the Trojans, looking out from the city,
may pour into the plain, fearless; but let some man,
a bold one, whom none among the Trojans knows,
remain outside the horse, setting a warlike heart in him,
who shall answer that the overweening might of the Achaeans
did the deed, in their longing for return, eager to escape,
crouching beneath the well-made horse; which they laboured to make
for Pallas, angered on behalf of the Trojan spearmen;
and let him declare this at length to those who question,
until they trust him, harsh though they are,
and lead him swiftly into the city, pitiable as he is,
that a grievous sign for our war may come to us,
to those men a smoking beacon raised swiftly aloft,
to the others a summons to come forth from the broad horse,
when the sons of Troy sleep heedless."
So he spoke; and all praised him; but beyond all others
Calchas marvelled at him, that he had set before the Achaeans
such cunning and a noble stratagem, which for the Argives was to be
a help to victory, but a great woe for the Trojans;
and therefore among the warlike chiefs he spoke:
"No longer now devise another stratagem in your minds,
O friends, but obey warlike Odysseus;
nor shall his counsel be vain, since he is wise of heart;
for already the gods are bringing the Danaans' desire to pass,
and signs unfulfilled appear from this side and that:
for above, through the clear sky, Zeus' thunders
crash together with the lightnings; and beside the host there dart
birds on the right, screaming with shrill cry.
But come, let us no longer for a long time about the city
remain; for great necessity has breathed into the Trojans
courage, which rouses even a worthless man toward war;
and men are strongest in battle then, when, staking their lives,
they take no heed of groaning destruction;
as now the sons of Troy, fearless, fight on
about their city; and the heart in them rages greatly."
To him as he spoke the mighty son of Achilles answered:
"O Calchas, against the foe brave men
fight face to face; but those within, shunning them from the towers,
are worthless and toil there, whose hearts fear oppresses;
therefore let us now devise neither stratagem nor any other
device; for it befits the best men to be men by toil
and by the spear; for bold warriors are better in battle."
To him as he spoke the might of the son of Laertes answered:
"O strong-hearted child of fearless Aeacides,
these things, as befits a noble blameless man,
you have gone through all very boldly, trusting in your hands;
but neither your unwearied father's dauntless valour
had strength to lay waste the prosperous city of Priam,
nor we, for all our much toiling; but come, more swiftly,
by the counsels of Calchas, going to the swift ships,
let us build a horse by the hands of Epeius,
who is by far the best among the Argives
for craftsmanship; and Athena taught him the work."
So he spoke; and all the chiefs obeyed him,
save warlike Neoptolemus; nor did the noble
mind of Philoctetes, who thought strong thoughts, persuade him;
for they were still insatiate of the wretched fray.
And they were eager to fight in the turmoil; and around the host,
their own men, they bade bring up about the boundless wall
all things that further strife in war,
hoping to lay waste the well-built town;
for both had come to the war by the counsels of the gods.
And now they would soon have accomplished all their hearts desired,
had not Zeus been wroth from the sky, and about the earth
made it quake beneath the Argives' feet, and shook together
all the air above, and cast the unwearied thunderbolt
before the heroes; and all Dardania
thundered in answer; and at once their noble purpose turned
to fear; and they forgot their strength and noble might,
and to famed Calchas, even unwilling, they yielded;
and they came to the ships with the Argives and the others,
in awe of the seer, who, they said, was of Zeus,
of Zeus or Phoebus; and they obeyed him in all things.

title: The Fall of Troy
text:
And when the gleaming stars wheeled round the sky,
shining on every side, and man forgets his toil,
then Athena, leaving the high seat of the blessed ones,
came in the likeness in all things of a tender-skinned maiden
to the ships and the host; and over the head of war-loved Epeius
she stood in a dream, and bade him
build a wooden horse; and she said that to him as he laboured
she herself would help, and herself would straightway come near,
urging him on to the work. And he, hearing the goddess' word,
exulting in his heart, leaped up from heedless sleep;
and he knew the immortal, deathless god; nor did his heart
ponder aught else, but kept his mind ever on the work
divine; and skilful craft went through his wits.
And when Dawn came, having thrust the kindly darkness
into Erebus, and the bright gleam went through the air,
then his divine dream did Epeius among the Argives,
as he had seen, as he had heard, tell to them in their longing;
and they, hearing him, rejoiced boundlessly.
And then the sons of Atreus sent swift men to come
to the flourishing glens of high-leaved Ida;
and they, falling upon the firs in the forest,
cut the tall trees; and the glens rang round
as they were struck; and the long peaks along the great mountains
were stripped of their thickets; and all the dell appeared,
no longer so lovely to the wild beasts as before;
and the trunks withered, longing for the force of the wind.
And the Achaeans, cleaving them with their axes,
swiftly bore them to the shores of the Hellespont
from the wooded mountain; and the spirit toiled at the work,
of the men and the mules; and the host laboured
unspeakably, each from his place serving Epeius;
for some cut with the jagged iron
the beams and measured out the planks; and others from the boughs
smoothed with axes the still-unsawn logs,
and each man did this thing or that, toiling; but Epeius
fashioned the feet of the wooden horse, and then
the belly, and on it above he fitted the back and the loins
behind, and the neck in front, and above the mane
he set upon the lofty neck, as though it truly
moved, and the shaggy head and the fair-haired tail,
the ears and the clear eyes and all else
by which a horse is moved; and the holy work grew
as of one truly living, since the god had given the man
lovely craft; and in three days all was finished
by the promptings of Pallas; and the great host of the Argives
rejoiced; and they marvelled how in the wood spirit
and swiftness of feet had been wrought, and it seemed to neigh.
And then noble Epeius, over the huge-bulked horse,
prayed to the unwearied Tritonian, stretching out his hands:
"Hear me, great-hearted goddess, and save me and your horse."
So he spoke; and the goddess of many counsels, Athena, heard him,
and made the work a wonder to all men on earth,
to all who saw it and who heard of it after.
But when the Danaans rejoiced, beholding the work of Epeius,
and the Trojans, terrified within their towers,
remained, shunning death and pitiless doom,
then at the streams of Ocean and the caves of Tethys,
when Zeus, high of heart, had gone apart from the gods,
strife fell upon the immortals; and their spirit was divided
as they were stirred; and mounting on the gusts of the winds
they were borne from heaven to earth; and beneath them the air
roared; and coming to the streams of Xanthus
they stood face to face against one another, some on the Achaeans'
side, others over the Trojans; and the lust of war fell on their hearts.
And with them gathered also those who held the broad sea.
And some, in anger, longed
to bring the guileful horse to nothing along with the ships, and others lovely
Ilium; but wily Fate held them back, and into turmoil
turned the minds of the blessed ones; and Ares began the fray,
and leaped against Athena; and so the others too
fell upon one another; and about them their immortal armour,
golden, as they moved, rang loud; and around them the broad
sea crashed; and the dark earth trembled
beneath the immortals' feet; and all together they shouted long.
And the terrible din reached up to the broad sky,
even to the pit of high-hearted Aïdoneus;
and the Titans beneath quaked greatly; and around them tall
Ida groaned, all of it, and the sounding streams
of the ever-flowing rivers, and with them the long ravines,
and the ships of the Argives and the famous city of Priam.
But there was no fear upon men; nor did they perceive,
by the gods' own promptings, their strife; and they, breaking off
peaks with their hands from the Idaean mountain,
hurled them at one another; but these, like grains of sand,
were easily scattered about the unyielding limbs of the gods,
breaking into little pieces. But at the ends of the earth from Zeus
his noble purpose did not escape; leaving at once the streams of Ocean
he went up to the broad sky; and him there bore
the East wind and the North, and with them the West and the South,
whom under a wondrous yoke gleaming Iris led,
of the car that is forever, which deathless Time fashioned for him
with unwearied hands out of unbreakable adamant.
And he came to the great peak of Olympus; and he shook
all the air above in his wrath; and from this side and that
the thunders crashed loud together with the lightnings; and the thunderbolts
fell thick upon the earth; and the air burned
unspeakably; and fear fell upon the immortals' hearts;
and the limbs of all trembled, immortal though they were.
And glorious Themis, in dread of them, swift as thought
leaped through the clouds; and quickly she reached them;
for she alone remained apart from the groaning fray;
and she spoke such a word, holding them back from fighting:
"Cease from the ill-sounding strife; for it does not befit you,
when Zeus is wroth, for the sake of short-lived men
to fight, you who are forever, since soon you all will be unseen;
for indeed from above upon you all the mountains
he will break into one, and neither sons nor daughters
will he spare, but all alike from above will he cover
with boundless earth; nor will there be escape for you
to the light; but grim gloom will hold you forever."
So she spoke; and they obeyed, trembling at Zeus' threat,
and ceased from the battle, and cast far away their wrath,
grievous as it was, and made friendship and concord;
and some went toward the sky, others into the sea,
and others remained on earth. And to the warlike Achaeans
the son of Laertes, shrewd of mind, spoke a word:
"O famed leaders of the Argives, strong of heart,
now in my longing give me proof, who are you
that are exceedingly strong and blameless; for now there comes
the work of necessity; but let us be mindful of Ares,
and go into the well-polished horse, that we may find
an end of the ill-sounding war; for thus it will be better
if by guile and grievous counsels
we sack the great city, for whose sake, having come hither,
we suffer many pains far from our dear land.
But come now, setting noble and valiant spirit in your minds . . .
for even in battle, beneath grim necessity,
a man, taking courage in his heart, has slain a better man,
though weaker born; for greatly does courage exalt the spirit,
which especially is glory for men.
But come, you chiefs, make ready the noble ambush;
and let the rest, going to the holy city of Tenedos,
remain, until the foe drag us to the city,
hoping to bring a gift to the Tritonian.
And let some noble warrior, whom the Trojans do not know well,
remain near the horse, setting an iron heart in him;
and let all be wholly steadfast in his care, all that I
have said before; and let him think nothing else in his mind,
that the Achaeans' deeds may not be made plain to the Trojans."
So he spoke; and Sinon answered him, a glorious man,
while the others feared; for a very great deed was he
to accomplish; therefore the broad host marvelled at him,
wise of heart; and he among them all spoke:
"O Odysseus, and all you noblest sons of the Achaeans,
this deed I will accomplish for you in your longing,
even if they maltreat me, and even if they purpose with fire
to cast me, alive as I am; for this is pleasing to my heart,
either to die by the hands of the foemen, or to escape,
bearing great glory to the Argives in their longing."
So he spoke boldly; and the Argives greatly rejoiced;
and one said: "How to this man a god has given great courage
today; for before he was not bold; but a god
urges him on, to become an evil to all the Trojans,
or to us both; for now I think, swiftly though it comes,
that the end of the grievous war will be unseen."
So spoke one among the host of the war-loving Achaeans;
and Nestor on the other side, urging them on, said:
"Now is there need, dear children, of strength and noble courage;
for now the gods are bringing to our longing hands
the end of toil and blameless victory;
but come, boldly, from within the capacious horse
go forth, since to mortals great courage grants glory;
would that great strength yet lay in my knees,
as when the son of Aeson, within his swift-faring ship
the Argo, called the chiefs, when I
was first of the chiefs eager to go down,
had not godlike Pelias held me back against my will;
but now grievous old age comes upon me; yet even so,
as a young man in his youth, I will go down within the horse
boldly; for courage will grant glory and renown."
To him as he spoke the son of fair-haired Achilles answered:
"O Nestor, you are foremost in mind of all
men; but pitiless old age has seized you round about,
nor is your strength steadfast, though you long for the toil;
therefore you must go back to the shores of Tenedos;
and into the ambush we young men, still insatiate of battle,
will go, as you, old man, bid us in our longing."
So he spoke; and the son of Neleus, coming close to him,
kissed both his hands and his head above,
because he had promised first to go down into the broad horse,
and bade him, the elder, remain outside
with the other Danaans; for he longed to toil;
and he addressed him, eager for the fray:
"You are of your father's might and kindly speech,
godlike Achilles; and I trust that by your hands
the Argives will sack the famed city of Priam;
late, after toil, great glory will be ours,
who have laboured much in the turmoil, with grievous pains;
for the gods set pains at the feet of men,
but noble things far off; and toil they set between;
therefore easy is the road for men into grievous misery,
but painful toward glory,
until one passes through the groaning toil with his feet."
So he spoke; and the glorious son of Achilles answered him:
"O old man, as you hope in your heart, so may it be
for us as we pray, since it is far better thus;
but if the gods will otherwise, let this too be borne;
for I would rather perish gloriously beneath Ares
than flee from Troy and bear many reproaches."
So speaking, he set upon his shoulders the immortal armour
of his father; and at once they too armed themselves,
the best of the heroes, all whose hearts were bold.
Tell me now, you Muses, as I ask of each one clearly,
all who went down into the capacious horse;
for you set all the song in my mind,
before yet the down was spread about my cheeks,
while I pastured my famed flocks in the plains of Smyrna,
thrice as far from the Hermus as a shouting man can be heard,
about the temple of Artemis in the Garden of Freedom,
on a hill neither too low nor very high.
First went down into the huge horse
the son of Achilles, and with him strong Menelaus
and Odysseus and Sthenelus and godlike Diomedes;
and Philoctetes went, and Anticlus, and Menestheus,
and with them high-hearted Thoas and fair-haired Polypoetes,
and Ajax and Eurypylus and Thrasymedes the godlike,
and Meriones and Idomeneus, both glorious,
and with them Podalirius of the good ashen spear, and Eurymachus,
and Teucer the godlike, and Ialmenus strong of heart,
and Thalpius and Antimachus and war-steadfast Leonteus;
and with them went godlike Eumelus and Euryalus
and Demophoon and Amphimachus and strong Agapenor,
and with them Acamas and Meges, son of mighty Phyleus;
and others went down, all who were the very best,
as many as the well-polished horse could hold within.
And among them last went down noble Epeius,
who had built the horse; and he knew in his own heart
both how to open its folds and to close them again;
therefore he went last of all; and he drew within
the ladders by which they had climbed; and, having fitted all firmly,
he sat there beside the bolt; and they in silence
all stayed between victory and destruction alike.
And the others sailed away with the ships over the broad sea,
having burned the huts where before they themselves had lain.
And over them two strong-hearted men ruled
and commanded, Nestor and the spearman Agamemnon;
and these too, though they longed to go down within the horse,
the Argives held back, that, remaining in the ships,
they might command the host, since it is far better that men
go about their work when their lords look on;
therefore they remained outside, chiefs though they were.
And they came swiftly to the shores of Tenedos;
and there they cast their anchors into the deep; and they themselves came out
of the ships in haste; and they bound their cables off
on the shores; and they themselves there remained at ease,
waiting until the beacon should appear to them in their longing.
And those in the horse were near the foe, now indeed
thinking they would perish, now that they would sack the holy city;
and upon their longing came the child of Morning.
The Trojans saw on the shores of the Hellespont
smoke still rising through the air; but they did not see the ships,
which had brought them from Hellas dire destruction.
And gladly all ran to the shore,
having put on their armour; for still fear held their hearts;
and they saw the well-polished horse; and about it
they stood in wonder; for a very great work had been wrought;
and near it again they saw ill-fated Sinon;
and questioning him about the Danaans, one from this side, one from that,
they ringed him round in the midst, standing about him; and at first with gentle
words they questioned him; but afterward with terrible
shouting; and long they tormented the guileful man,
ever for a long time; but he, firm as a rock,
remained, clothed about with unyielding limbs; and at last
they cut from his body alike his ears and his nose,
maiming him utterly, that he might speak the truth,
where the Danaans had gone with their ships, and whether the horse
held aught within. But he, setting strength in his heart,
heeded not the unseemly outrage, but in his spirit
endured both the blows and being tortured in the fire
grievously; for Hera breathed great strength into him;
and such guileful words he spoke in their midst:
"The Argives are fleeing in their ships over the sea,
worn out by the long war and the misery;
and by the will of Calchas, for warlike Tritogeneia,
they built the horse, that they might escape the wrath of the goddess,
who was utterly enraged on behalf of the Trojans; and concerning their return,
by the promptings of Odysseus they purposed my destruction,
that they might slay me beside the ill-sounding sea
for the deities of the deep. But it did not escape me, but the grievous
libations and the barley-meal I swiftly shunned,
and by the will of the immortals I fell down at the feet of the horse;
and they, though unwilling, of necessity left me,
in awe of the strong-hearted daughter of great Zeus."
So he spoke with cunning, and his heart did not weary under pains;
for it belongs to a strong man to endure evil necessity.
And some throughout the host believed him; but others said
he was a wily deceiver, to whom the counsel
of Laocoon was pleasing; for he, speaking wise words,
said it was a dire stratagem by the promptings of the Achaeans,
and urged all swiftly to burn the horse,
the wooden horse, and to learn if it hid anything.
And now they would have obeyed him and escaped destruction,
had not Tritogeneia, wroth in her heart
against him and the Trojans and the city, shaken the earth beneath
divinely, beneath the feet of Laocoon.
And straightway fear fell upon him; trembling broke the limbs
of the high-hearted man; and over his head black
night was poured; and a hateful pain fell upon his eyelids,
and confounded the man's eyes beneath his shaggy brows;
and his eyeballs, pierced with grievous pains,
were stirred from their roots; and his pupils whirled about,
tormented within; and grievous anguish came
even to the membranes and the foundations of the brain;
and at one time his eyes seemed mingled with much blood,
at another, hard to heal, gleaming pale;
and often they ran, as when from a hard rock
water trickles down from the mountains, mixed with snow;
and he was like a madman, and saw all things double,
groaning terribly. And still he urged the Trojans on,
nor heeded his torment; and the noble light from him took
the divine goddess; and beneath his eyelids his eyes stood white
from the deadly blood; and the host groaned round about,
pitying the dear man, and dreading the immortal Driver-of-Spoil,
lest in his folly he had somehow offended,
and within them their mind was bent toward dire destruction,
fearing lest grief follow upon them too,
because they had maltreated the body of wretched Sinon,
hoping in their hearts that he would tell all things truly;
therefore they led him eagerly into the Trojan city,
pitying him at last. And all gathering together
quickly cast a rope about the huge horse,
binding it above, since for it noble Epeius
had set beneath its sturdy feet well-running wheels,
that it might follow the men toward the city,
dragged by the hands of the Trojans. And all together
they hauled, bearing down in a throng, as when a ship
men drag with toil into the sounding sea,
the men, and the sturdy rollers groan round about,
worn down, and dreadfully the keel, creaking on every side,
slips and goes down into the swell of the sea;
so they, their own bane, the work of Epeius, toward the city
with all their force, toiling, hauled up; and about it
they set in plenty a flourishing adornment of garlands;
and themselves they crowned their heads; and loud the flutes blew,
calling one to another; and Enyo laughed,
beholding the evil end of war; and on high Hera
took delight; and Athena rejoiced; and they, coming
to their own city, the veil of the great town
loosed, and led in the baneful horse; and the women of Troy
raised a cry, and all, standing round and gazing,
marvelled at the mighty work; but it hid from them their bane.

title: The Fall of Troy
text:
And Laocoon still remained, urging his comrades
to bring the horse to nothing with consuming fire; but they in no way
obeyed him, for they dreaded the immortals' threat.
And against him the great-hearted goddess Athena
devised another deed yet more cruel for the wretched children of Laocoon.
For there was a cave beneath a rugged rock,
misty, untrodden by mortals, in which terrible
beasts dwelt, of the still deadly brood
of Typhon, in the folds of the island which men
call Calydne, in the sea over against Troy.
Thence she roused the might of the serpents and called them
to Troy; and they, straightway stirred by the goddess,
shook the whole island; and the sea crashed round
as they went, and the wave parted; and they were borne on,
darting out their dread tongues; and the monsters of the sea shuddered;
and round about loudly groaned the daughters of Xanthus,
the nymphs, and of Simoeis; and from Olympus Cypris
grieved; and they swiftly came where the goddess urged them,
whetting on their grim jaws the bane of their teeth
against the wretched children; and evil panic came over
the Trojans, when they saw the dread monsters through the city;
nor did any of the warriors, even one of fearless might,
dare to stay; for pitiless dread held them all
